maths/probability-statistics.html:
Moment Generating Functions — Encoding All Moments

The moment generating function (MGF) of a random variable X is defined as M_X(t) = E[etX] for those real t where the expectation exists. For a discrete variable the sum Σ etx P(X=x) is used; for a continuous variable the integral ∫ etx f(x) dx applies. The MGF, when it exists in a neighbourhood of zero, uniquely determines the distribution — two random variables with identical MGFs on an interval containing 0 have the same distribution. This uniqueness property makes the MGF a powerful tool for identifying distributions of sums of independent variables: if X and Y are independent, MX+Y(t) = M_X(t) M_Y(t). The product form turns convolution of densities into simple multiplication, which is why the MGF is the standard device for proving that the sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson, the sum of independent normals is normal, and the sum of independent gamma variables with the same scale parameter is gamma.

Moments are recovered by differentiation: the k‑th raw moment E[X^k] equals the k‑th derivative of M_X(t) evaluated at t=0, provided the derivative exists. For example, the MGF of a binomial(n,p) variable is (1-p+pe^t)^n. Differentiating once gives np, differentiating twice gives np(1-p)+n2p2, from which the variance np(1-p) follows immediately. The MGF of a normal(μ,σ2) variable is exp(μt + ½σ2t2); its first derivative at 0 is μ, second derivative is μ2+σ2, yielding variance σ2. When the MGF does not exist (e.g., Cauchy distribution), characteristic functions φ_X(t)=E[eitX] serve the same purpose because they always exist. In JEE‑level problems, the MGF is most often used to identify a distribution from a given functional form or to compute moments of a sum without performing convolution integrals.

A common examiner twist is to give the MGF of a random variable and ask for a probability such as P(X=2) or P(X>1). The student must recognise the MGF as that of a known distribution, write down its parameters, and then use the PMF or CDF of that distribution. Another twist: given M_X(t) = (0.3+0.7e^t)5, identify X ~ Binomial(5,0.7) and compute P(X≥3) = Σk=35 C(5,k) 0.7^k 0.35-k. Mastery of the standard MGFs — Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson, exponential, gamma, normal — and the product rule for independence is essential for rapid problem solving.

Central Limit Theorem — Why the Normal Appears Everywhere

The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) states that for a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables X1, X2, … with finite mean μ and finite variance σ2, the standardized sum (Σi=1^n X_i - nμ) / (σ√n) converges in distribution to a standard normal N(0,1) as n → ∞. In practical terms, for moderately large n (often n ≥ 30 is quoted, but the required n depends on the skewness of the underlying distribution), the distribution of the sample mean X is approximately N(μ, σ2/n). This approximation underpins most large‑sample inference: confidence intervals for means, hypothesis tests about means, and the normal approximation to the binomial and Poisson distributions.

The CLT does not require the original variables to be normal; it only requires independence, identical distribution, and finite variance. Heavy‑tailed distributions with infinite variance (e.g., Cauchy) violate the conditions, and the sample mean does not converge to a normal law. The rate of convergence is governed by the Berry‑Esseen theorem, which bounds the supremum distance between the CDF of the standardized sum and the standard normal CDF by a constant times the third absolute moment divided by σ3√n. This explains why highly skewed distributions (exponential, log‑normal) need larger n for a good normal approximation.

In JEE problems, the CLT is frequently invoked to approximate probabilities for sums or averages of many i.i.d. variables. A typical question: "A fair die is rolled 100 times. Approximate the probability that the total score exceeds 370." Here each roll has mean 3.5 and variance 35/12 ≈ 2.917. The sum has mean 350 and variance 100×35/12 ≈ 291.7, standard deviation ≈ 17.08. The standardized value for 370.5 (continuity correction) is (370.5-350)/17.08 ≈ 1.20, giving probability ≈ 0.115. The continuity correction is crucial when approximating a discrete sum by a continuous normal. Another common variant uses the CLT to approximate a binomial(n,p) by N(np, np(1-p)) when np and n(1-p) are both >5, again with continuity correction.

Technique
A factory produces bolts whose lengths are independent with mean 5.0 cm and standard deviation 0.2 cm. A random sample of 64 bolts is taken. Approximate the probability that the sample mean length lies between 4.98 cm and 5.02 cm.
The sample mean X of n=64 i.i.d. observations has mean μ = 5.0 and standard deviation σ/√n = 0.2/8 = 0.025. By the CLT, X ≈ N(5.0, 0.0252). Standardize the bounds: z1 = (4.98 - 5.0)/0.025 = -0.8; z2 = (5.02 - 5.0)/0.025 = 0.8. Using standard normal tables, P(-0.8 < Z < 0.8) = Φ(0.8) - Φ(-0.8) = 0.7881 - 0.2119 = 0.5762. Hence the approximate probability is 0.576.
Exam Day Strategy
When a problem asks for an approximation using the CLT, always check whether the sample size is large enough (np and n(1-p) > 5 for binomial, or n ≥ 30 for general distributions). Apply continuity correction for discrete underlying variables. Write down the mean and standard deviation of the sum or average explicitly before standardizing; this avoids arithmetic slips and shows the examiner you understand the scaling.

Sampling Distributions — Chi‑Square, t, and F

Sampling distributions describe the behaviour of statistics computed from random samples. Three fundamental sampling distributions arise from normal samples: the chi‑square, Student's t, and Snedecor's F. If Z1,…,Z_k are independent standard normals, then Q = Σi=1^k Z_i2 follows a chi‑square distribution with k degrees of freedom, denoted χ2_k. Its mean is k and variance 2k. If a random sample X1,…,X_n is drawn from N(μ,σ2), then (n-1)S2/σ2 ∼ χ2n-1, where S2 is the sample variance. This result is the basis for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for a single variance.

Student's t distribution emerges when the population variance is unknown. Let X be the sample mean and S the sample standard deviation from a normal sample of size n. Then T = (X - μ) / (S/√n) follows a t distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom. The t density is symmetric, bell‑shaped, but with heavier tails than the normal; as n→∞, tn-1 → N(0,1). The t distribution is used for confidence intervals and tests about a single mean when σ is unknown, and for the difference of two means from independent normal samples with equal variances (pooled t) or unequal variances (Welch's t).

The F distribution is the ratio of two independent chi‑square variables divided by their degrees of freedom: F = (U/df1) / (V/df2) where U∼χ2df1, V∼χ2df2 independent. If two independent normal samples have variances σ12 and σ22, then (S12/σ12) / (S22/σ22) ∼ Fn1-1, n2-1. This underlies the test for equality of two variances and the analysis of variance (ANOVA) for comparing several means. In JEE, the F distribution appears mainly in the context of comparing two sample variances or in regression ANOVA tables. Critical values for χ2, t, and F are tabulated; the exam may provide a small excerpt or expect you to know that for large df the distributions approach normal or chi‑square limits.

Hypothesis Testing — Framework and Decision Rules

Statistical hypothesis testing formalises the decision between a null hypothesis H0 and an alternative H1 using sample data. The procedure: (1) State H0 and H1. (2) Choose a significance level α (commonly 0.05 or 0.01). (3) Select an appropriate test statistic whose sampling distribution under H0 is known (e.g., Z, t, χ2, F). (4) Determine the critical region (rejection region) such that P(test statistic falls in critical region | H0 true) = α. (5) Compute the observed value of the test statistic from the sample. (6) Reject H0 if the observed value lies in the critical region; otherwise do not reject H0. The p‑value is the smallest α at which H0 would be rejected; it equals the probability, under H0, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one.

Type I error (rejecting a true H0) has probability α. Type II error (failing to reject a false H0) has probability β; power = 1-β. The Neyman‑Pearson lemma shows that for simple hypotheses, the most powerful test at level α is based on the likelihood ratio. For composite hypotheses, uniformly most powerful tests rarely exist; instead we use likelihood ratio tests, Wald tests, or score tests. In JEE, the focus is on the classical tests: Z‑test for a mean with known variance, t‑test for a mean with unknown variance, χ2‑test for a variance, and F‑test for equality of two variances. Two‑sample problems use pooled or Welch t‑tests for means, and the F‑test for variances. The exam may also test the chi‑square goodness‑of‑fit test or test of independence in contingency tables, where the test statistic Σ (O_i - E_i)2 / E_i follows χ2 with appropriate df.

A frequent examiner twist is to ask for the interpretation of a p‑value or the consequence of changing α. Remember: a small p‑value indicates strong evidence against H0, but it is not the probability that H0 is true. Also, failing to reject H0 does not prove H0; it merely indicates insufficient evidence. When constructing confidence intervals, the duality with two‑sided tests holds: a 1-α confidence interval contains exactly those parameter values that would not be rejected by a two‑sided test at level α.

Conditional Expectation and the Law of Total Variance

Conditional expectation E[Y|X] is a function of the random variable X; it is the best predictor of Y in the mean‑square sense given X. For discrete variables, E[Y|X=x] = Σ_y y P(Y=y|X=x); for continuous, the integral with the conditional density. Two fundamental identities are the law of total expectation (iterated expectation): E[Y] = E[ E[Y|X] ], and the law of total variance: Var(Y) = E[ Var(Y|X) ] + Var( E[Y|X] ). The first term is the average of the conditional variances (within‑group variability); the second term is the variance of the conditional means (between‑group variability). This decomposition is the probabilistic analogue of ANOVA and is extremely useful for computing variances of mixture distributions or hierarchical models.

Example: Suppose N ∼ Poisson(λ) and, given N=n, X1,…,X_n are i.i.d. with mean μ and variance σ2, independent of N. Let S = Σi=1^N X_i (with S=0 if N=0). Then E[S|N] = Nμ, Var(S|N) = Nσ2. By total expectation, E[S] = E[N]μ = λμ. By total variance, Var(S) = E[Nσ2] + Var(Nμ) = λσ2 + λμ2 = λ(σ2+μ2). This matches the known variance of a compound Poisson distribution. Another classic use: if X|Y=y ∼ N(y,1) and Y ∼ N(0,τ2), then E[X|Y]=Y, Var(X|Y)=1. Hence E[X]=E[Y]=0, Var(X)=E[1]+Var(Y)=1+τ2. The law of total variance avoids the need to derive the marginal density of X explicitly.

In JEE problems, conditional expectation often appears in the context of the "random sum" or "random number of trials" models. Recognising the structure E[ Σi=1^N X_i ] = E[N] E[X] (when N is independent of the X_i's) and Var( Σi=1^N X_i ) = E[N] Var(X) + Var(N) (E[X])2 is a direct application of the two laws. The examiner may also test the property that for any random variables X,Y, Cov(X,Y) = Cov( X, E[Y|X] ), which follows from the law of total covariance. Mastery of these identities allows rapid solution of problems that would otherwise require messy double sums or integrals.

  • Assuming the MGF exists for all t when it only exists in a neighbourhood of zero.
  • Forgetting the continuity correction when using the normal approximation to a discrete sum.
  • Using the chi‑square test for variance without verifying the underlying normality assumption.
  • Confusing the p‑value with the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
  • Applying the law of total variance without checking that the conditioning variable is independent of the summands where required.
  • Treating the t‑distribution as normal for small sample sizes (n < 30) when the population variance is unknown.
  • Review these traps before the exam to avoid common pitfalls.

hand/calc-variations.html:
Second Variation and Sufficient Conditions for Minima

The first variation yields the Euler‑Lagrange equation, a necessary condition for an extremum. To decide whether a stationary function is a minimum, maximum, or saddle, one examines the second variation δ²J. For a functional J[y]=∫ₐᵇ L(x,y,y') dx with fixed endpoints, the second variation takes the quadratic form δ²J = ∫ₐᵇ (P η'² + Q η²) dx where η is an admissible variation vanishing at the endpoints, P = ∂²L/∂y'² evaluated on the extremal, and Q = ∂²L/∂y² − d/dx(∂²L/∂y∂y'). The Legendre necessary condition for a weak minimum requires P ≥ 0 on [a,b]; for a strong minimum the strengthened Legendre condition P > 0 is needed. Even if Legendre holds, the extremal may fail to be a minimum if there exists a conjugate point — a point c ∈ (a,b] where a nontrivial solution of the Jacobi accessory equation (P u')' − Q u = 0 vanishes at both a and c. Jacobi's theorem states that a weak minimum occurs iff the strengthened Legendre condition holds and the interval contains no conjugate points. For strong minima one also needs the Weierstrass excess function E(x,y,y',p) = L(x,y,p) − L(x,y,y') − (p−y')∂L/∂y' to be nonnegative for all admissible p. These criteria together give a complete sufficient framework: strengthened Legendre, no conjugate points, and Weierstrass condition guarantee a strong local minimum.

In practice, checking the Jacobi condition reduces to solving a linear second‑order ODE along the extremal. For the brachistochrone, the extremal is a cycloid and the accessory equation can be solved explicitly, showing no conjugate points before the endpoint, confirming the cycloid is a true minimum time curve. For the catenary, the second variation is positive definite, and the absence of conjugate points follows from the convexity of the hyperbolic cosine. In problems with variable endpoints, the Jacobi condition must be supplemented by transversality conditions at the free boundaries. The second variation also underpins the direct method: convexity of L in y' (i.e., P ≥ 0) ensures lower semicontinuity of the functional in Sobolev spaces, which is the key hypothesis for existence of minimizers via the Tonelli‑Hilbert direct method.

Advanced applications involve the Morse index theorem, which relates the number of negative eigenvalues of the second variation operator to the number of conjugate points. This connects variational calculus to spectral theory and has implications for stability of solutions in nonlinear PDEs. In optimal control, the second variation leads to the generalized Legendre‑Clebsch condition, a cornerstone for verifying second‑order optimality in Pontryagin's framework.

Corner Conditions and Weierstrass‑Erdmann Conditions

Extremals of variational problems are not always smooth; they may contain corners where y' has a jump discontinuity. The classical derivation of the Euler‑Lagrange equation assumes y ∈ C², but many physical problems (e.g., refraction of light, elastic strings with point loads) produce piecewise smooth extremals. At a corner point c ∈ (a,b) the function y is continuous but y' may have distinct left and right limits y'₋ and y'₊. The first variation, when integrated by parts on each subinterval, yields boundary terms at c that must vanish independently. This gives the Weierstrass‑Erdmann corner conditions: ∂L/∂y' evaluated from the left equals ∂L/∂y' evaluated from the right, and the quantity L − y' ∂L/∂y' is also continuous across the corner. These two scalar equations are necessary for a piecewise C¹ function to be an extremal. They are the direct analogue of Snell's law in optics: the momentum conjugate to the coordinate is conserved across the interface.

If the Lagrangian does not depend explicitly on x, the second corner condition reduces to conservation of the Hamiltonian H = y' ∂L/∂y' − L across the corner. For the brachistochrone with a piecewise constant gravitational field, the corner conditions determine the angle change at the interface. In problems with a discontinuous Lagrangian (e.g., a particle moving in a medium with a sharp change in refractive index), the corner conditions replace the Euler‑Lagrange equation at the discontinuity. The Weierstrass excess function also plays a role: a strong minimum requires E ≥ 0 for all admissible slopes on both sides of the corner. If E becomes negative for some slope, the corner can be "rounded" to lower the functional, indicating the piecewise extremal is not a strong minimizer.

Corner conditions extend to higher‑order problems and to functionals depending on higher derivatives. For a functional involving y'', the natural corner conditions involve continuity of ∂L/∂y'' and ∂L/∂y' − d/dx(∂L/∂y''). In the calculus of variations on manifolds, corners correspond to geodesics with broken directions, and the corner conditions become the requirement that the momentum covector be parallel transported across the break. These ideas are essential in the study of minimal surfaces with free boundaries and in the numerical treatment of variational problems where mesh adaptation creates piecewise polynomial approximations.

Weierstrass‑Erdmann corner conditions
Consider the functional J[y] = ∫₀² (y'² + y²) dx with y(0)=0, y(2)=1. Suppose an extremal has a corner at x=1. Find the piecewise linear extremal satisfying the corner conditions.
On each subinterval the Euler‑Lagrange equation is y'' − y = 0, whose general solution is y = A eˣ + B e⁻ˣ. Let y₁(x)=A₁ eˣ + B₁ e⁻ˣ on [0,1] and y₂(x)=A₂ eˣ + B₂ e⁻ˣ on [1,2]. Boundary conditions: y₁(0)=0 ⇒ A₁ + B₁ = 0. y₂(2)=1 ⇒ A₂ e² + B₂ e⁻² = 1. Continuity at x=1: y₁(1)=y₂(1) ⇒ A₁ e + B₁ e⁻¹ = A₂ e + B₂ e⁻¹. Corner conditions: ∂L/∂y' = 2y' continuous ⇒ y₁'(1)=y₂'(1) ⇒ A₁ e − B₁ e⁻¹ = A₂ e − B₂ e⁻¹. The second condition L − y'∂L/∂y' = y² − y'² continuous gives the same equation because L = y'² + y² and ∂L/∂y' = 2y', so L − y'∂L/∂y' = y² − y'². Solving the four linear equations yields A₁ = (e²−1)/(2(e⁴−1)), B₁ = −A₁, A₂ = (e⁴−e²)/(2(e⁴−1)), B₂ = (e²−1)/(2(e⁴−1)). The extremal is thus piecewise exponential, satisfying all corner conditions.
Exam‑day strategy
When a problem allows a corner, first write the Euler‑Lagrange equation on each smooth segment. Then impose continuity of the function and the two Weierstrass‑Erdmann quantities. Remember that if L is independent of x, the second condition is simply Hamiltonian continuity. Check the Weierstrass excess function sign to decide whether the corner is a strong minimizer. Practice with piecewise constant Lagrangians (e.g., Snell's law) to internalise the pattern.

Variable Endpoint Problems and Transversality Conditions

In many applications the endpoints of the extremal are not fixed but lie on given curves or surfaces. The classical fixed‑endpoint problem assumes y(a)=α, y(b)=β. If the right endpoint is free to move along a curve φ(x,y)=0, the first variation acquires an extra boundary term (∂L/∂y' δy + (L − y' ∂L/∂y') δx) evaluated at the endpoint. Requiring this term to vanish for all admissible variations (δx, δy) tangent to the constraint curve yields the transversality condition: (L − y' ∂L/∂y') φₓ + ∂L/∂y' φ_y = 0 at the endpoint, where φₓ, φ_y are partial derivatives of the constraint. Geometrically, this says the momentum covector (∂L/∂y', −H) is orthogonal to the tangent of the endpoint curve. If the endpoint is completely free (no constraint), both δx and δy are arbitrary, giving the natural boundary conditions ∂L/∂y' = 0 and L − y' ∂L/∂y' = 0 at that endpoint.

For problems with both endpoints variable on curves φ₁(x,y)=0 and φ₂(x,y)=0, one obtains two transversality conditions, one at each end. These conditions replace the fixed‑endpoint Dirichlet conditions and are essential in problems such as the shortest path from a point to a curve (the geodesic meets the curve orthogonally in the metric induced by L) or the brachistochrone with a free terminal point on a given curve. In optimal control, transversality conditions become the terminal conditions for the adjoint variables: if the terminal state is constrained to a manifold, the costate vector must be orthogonal to the tangent space of that manifold.

The transversality conditions also appear in the Hamilton‑Jacobi theory: the generating function S(x,y) satisfies ∂S/∂x = −H, ∂S/∂y = p, and the condition that the extremal meets the endpoint curve translates into a boundary condition for S. In the direct method, variable endpoints are handled by extending the admissible space to include functions defined on variable intervals, often via a reparameterisation that maps all intervals to a fixed reference domain. The lower semicontinuity arguments then require the Lagrangian to be convex in (y', y) uniformly with respect to the endpoint positions.

Isoperimetric Problems and Lagrange Multipliers

An isoperimetric problem seeks to extremize a functional J[y] = ∫ₐᵇ L(x,y,y') dx subject to an integral constraint K[y] = ∫ₐᵇ M(x,y,y') dx = constant, with fixed endpoints. The classical example is Dido's problem: maximize the area enclosed by a curve of given length. The method of Lagrange multipliers extends to functionals: one forms the augmented functional J̃[y] = ∫ₐᵇ (L + λ M) dx, where λ is a constant multiplier. The Euler‑Lagrange equation for the augmented Lagrangian L̃ = L + λ M gives the necessary condition for a constrained extremum. The multiplier λ is determined by the constraint K[y] = constant together with the boundary conditions.

If the constraint is a differential equation (holonomic or nonholonomic), the multiplier becomes a function λ(x) and the augmented Lagrangian is L + λ(x) M. The Euler‑Lagrange equations then form a coupled system for y and λ. For nonholonomic constraints (e.g., a rolling disk), the multiplier method yields the correct equations of motion only when the constraints are linear in velocities; otherwise the vakonomic (variational) and nonholonomic (mechanical) approaches differ. The isoperimetric problem also admits a second‑order analysis: the second variation of the augmented functional must be positive definite on the subspace of variations satisfying the linearised constraint ∫ (∂M/∂y η + ∂M/∂y' η') dx = 0. This leads to a modified Jacobi condition where the accessory equation includes the multiplier term.

Applications abound: the shape of a hanging chain of fixed length (catenary with length constraint), the optimal shape of a beam under a volume constraint, and the principal eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian (Rayleigh quotient). In the calculus of variations on manifolds, isoperimetric problems become the study of minimal submanifolds with prescribed volume, leading to the concept of constant mean curvature surfaces. The Lagrange multiplier λ acquires a physical meaning: in the catenary it is the horizontal tension; in the eigenvalue problem it is the eigenvalue itself. Modern treatments use the language of constrained critical points on Banach manifolds, where the Lagrange multiplier theorem is a consequence of the implicit function theorem in infinite dimensions.

Optimal Control and Pontryagin Maximum Principle

Optimal control theory generalises the calculus of variations by allowing the control variable u(t) to appear explicitly and by admitting inequality constraints on state and control. The problem: minimize J = ∫₀ᵀ L(x,u,t) dt subject to ẋ = f(x,u,t), x(0)=x₀, x(T) free or constrained, and u(t) ∈ U (a closed set). The Hamiltonian is defined as H(x,p,u,t) = p·f(x,u,t) − L(x,u,t), where p(t) is the costate (adjoint) vector. Pontryagin's Maximum Principle (PMP) states that if (x*,u*) is optimal, there exists a nontrivial absolutely continuous costate p(t) such that: (1) ẋ* = ∂H/∂p, ṗ = −∂H/∂x (Hamilton's equations); (2) H(x*,p,u*,t) = maxu∈U H(x*,p,u,t) for almost every t; (3) transversality conditions at the terminal time: p(T) = ∂Φ/∂x if the terminal cost Φ(x(T)) is present, or p(T) orthogonal to the terminal manifold if x(T) is constrained. The maximisation condition replaces the stationary condition ∂H/∂u = 0 of the unconstrained calculus of variations and allows bang‑bang controls where the optimal u switches between extreme points of U.

The PMP reduces to the Euler‑Lagrange equation when U = ℝᵐ and the Hamiltonian is concave in u; then the maximum is attained at ∂H/∂u = 0, which is exactly the Legendre transform relation p = ∂L/∂u. For problems with state constraints (e.g., x(t) ≥ 0), the costate may have jumps, and the Hamiltonian is continuous but not necessarily differentiable. The theory of needle variations and the construction of the adjoint equation via the Hamiltonian formalism provide a rigorous foundation. The PMP also yields the Hamilton‑Jacobi‑Bellman equation in dynamic programming: the value function V(x,t) satisfies −∂V/∂t = maxu∈U { −L + ∂V/∂x·f }. The viscosity solution concept resolves non‑smoothness of V.

In practice, solving a PMP problem involves a two‑point boundary value problem for (x,p) with the control determined by the maximisation condition. Numerical methods include shooting, collocation, and direct transcription (which discretises the control and state and solves a large nonlinear program). The PMP is the cornerstone of modern optimal control, underpinning applications in aerospace trajectory optimisation, robotics, economics (optimal growth), and quantum control. Its geometric formulation on the cotangent bundle shows that optimal trajectories are projections of Hamiltonian flows, linking back to the symplectic structure of Hamiltonian mechanics discussed earlier.

  • Confusing the Legendre necessary condition (P ≥ 0) with the strengthened Legendre condition (P > 0) for strong minima.
  • Forgetting that the Weierstrass‑Erdmann corner conditions require continuity of both ∂L/∂y' and L − y'∂L/∂y', not just the momentum.
  • Applying the transversality condition for a free endpoint as ∂L/∂y' = 0 only, while neglecting the Hamiltonian continuity L − y'∂L/∂y' = 0.
  • Treating the Lagrange multiplier in an isoperimetric problem as a function of x when the constraint is an integral (it is a constant).
  • Assuming the Pontryagin Maximum Principle's maximisation condition is equivalent to ∂H/∂u = 0 even when the control set U has boundaries.
  • Overlooking the need to check the Weierstrass excess function E ≥ 0 for strong minimality after finding a candidate extremal.
  • Misidentifying conjugate points by solving the Jacobi equation with incorrect boundary conditions (must vanish at the left endpoint and at the candidate conjugate point).

These advanced topics complete the toolkit for tackling graduate‑level variational problems and optimal control questions in competitive examinations.

hand/perverse-sheaves.html:
Weight Filtration and the Mixed Hodge Module Formalism

Morihiko Saito’s theory of mixed Hodge modules (1990) provides a Hodge‑theoretic lift of the category of perverse sheaves. For a complex algebraic variety X, the abelian category MHM(X) of mixed Hodge modules is equipped with a weight filtration W• such that the associated graded pieces Gr^W_k are pure Hodge modules of weight k. The forgetful functor rat: MHM(X) → Perv(X, ℚ) sending a mixed Hodge module to its underlying perverse sheaf is exact and faithful. The weight filtration on a mixed Hodge module M induces a filtration on the perverse sheaf rat(M) which coincides with the perverse Leray filtration for a proper morphism. In particular, for a proper map f: X → Y, the decomposition theorem Rf_* IC_X ≅ ⊕ ICZ_k(L_k)[d_k] lifts to an isomorphism in the derived category of mixed Hodge modules, and the summands inherit pure Hodge structures of weight dim Z_k. This Hodge‑theoretic refinement explains why the intersection cohomology groups IH^i(X) carry pure Hodge structures of weight i, a fact that cannot be seen at the level of perverse sheaves alone. The construction uses the nearby and vanishing cycle functors ψ_f, φ_f on mixed Hodge modules, which are compatible with the corresponding functors on perverse sheaves and preserve the weight filtration. Saito’s proof relies on the strictness of the Hodge filtration for the de Rham complex of a regular holonomic D‑module, a deep analytic result due to Kashiwara and Kawai. The mixed Hodge module formalism also yields a canonical extension of the weight filtration to the derived category D^b MHM(X), making it a filtered triangulated category. This framework is essential for modern applications such as the proof of the Kähler package for intersection cohomology and the study of motivic weights in the geometric Langlands program.

The Decomposition Theorem in Families and the Relative Hard Lefschetz

The Beilinson–Bernstein–Deligne–Gabber decomposition theorem extends from a single proper morphism to a family of proper morphisms. Let f: X → S be a proper morphism of complex algebraic varieties with S smooth and connected. For each s ∈ S, the fiber f_s: X_s → Y_s satisfies Rfs* ICX_s ≅ ⊕_k ICZk,s(Lk,s)[d_k]. The theorem asserts that the formation of this decomposition commutes with base change: the direct sum decomposition of Rf_* IC_X in D^b_c(Y) is locally constant in the analytic topology on S. This local constancy is a consequence of the relative hard Lefschetz theorem. For a relatively ample line bundle L on X/S, the cup product L^k: R-kf_* IC_X → Rkf_* IC_X is an isomorphism of perverse sheaves on Y for all k. The proof uses the theory of polarizable Hodge modules: the relative hard Lefschetz isomorphism is induced by a morphism of mixed Hodge modules which is strict with respect to the Hodge and weight filtrations. As a corollary, the perverse cohomology sheaves ^pH^i(Rf_* IC_X) are semisimple local systems on a dense open subset of Y, and their monodromy representations are completely reducible. This semisimplicity is the geometric incarnation of the fact that the monodromy of the Gauss–Manin connection on the intersection cohomology of the fibers is semisimple. The relative hard Lefschetz also implies the relative Hodge–Riemann bilinear relations, which give a positive definite pairing on the primitive parts of the perverse cohomology. These results have been used by de Cataldo and Migliorini to prove the topological invariance of intersection cohomology Betti numbers for projective morphisms and to establish the hard Lefschetz theorem for the intersection cohomology of singular projective varieties.

Worked Example: Relative Hard Lefschetz for a Family of Nodal Curves
Let π: C → Δ be a proper flat family of curves over the unit disc Δ such that the generic fiber C_t (t ≠ 0) is smooth of genus g and the central fiber C0 is a nodal curve with a single node. Let L be a relatively ample line bundle on C. Show that the cup product L: R-1π_* IC_C → R1π_* IC_C is an isomorphism of perverse sheaves on Δ.
The intersection complex IC_C on the total space C is the shifted constant sheaf ℚ_C[2] because C is a surface with at worst a nodal singularity in the central fiber; the node is a rational double point, so IC_C = ℚ_C[2]. The higher direct images R^iπ_* ℚ_C[2] are perverse sheaves on Δ. For i = -1, R-1π_* ℚ_C[2] = R1π_* ℚ_C[1] is the local system on Δ* given by H1(C_t, ℚ) extended across 0 as the nearby cycles ψ_π ℚ_C[2]. For i = 1, R1π_* ℚ_C[2] = R3π_* ℚ_C[1] is the dual local system by Verdier duality. The relatively ample line bundle L restricts to an ample line bundle on each fiber, giving a Lefschetz operator L: H1(C_t) → H3(C_t) ≅ H1(C_t)^∨. By the classical hard Lefschetz theorem on the smooth fibers, this is an isomorphism for t ≠ 0. The relative hard Lefschetz theorem (Saito, 1990) asserts that this isomorphism extends across the singular fiber because the morphism of mixed Hodge modules induced by L is strict. Hence the map of perverse sheaves L: R-1π_* IC_C → R1π_* IC_C is an isomorphism on Δ.
Exam Strategy: Recognising Relative Hard Lefschetz in Disguise
Questions often ask for the isomorphism type of Rf_* IC_X for a projective morphism f. If the morphism is a family over a curve, the relative hard Lefschetz forces the perverse cohomology sheaves to be semisimple local systems. Look for keywords such as “relatively ample”, “proper flat family”, or “semisimple monodromy”. The answer is usually a direct sum of intersection complexes of subvarieties of the base twisted by semisimple local systems. Do not confuse this with the ordinary hard Lefschetz on a single variety, which concerns the cohomology of the variety itself.

Perverse Sheaves on Stratified Spaces and Verdier Duality

Verdier duality D_X: D^b_c(X) → D^b_c(X) is an anti‑equivalence of triangulated categories sending a constructible complex ℱ to Rℋom(ℱ, ω_X), where ω_X is the dualizing complex. On a smooth variety of dimension n, ω_X ≅ ℚ_X[2n]; on a singular variety, ω_X is the intersection cohomology complex IC_X shifted by the dimension. The perverse t‑structure is self‑dual: D_X(Perv(X)) = Perv(X). This means that for any perverse sheaf P, its Verdier dual D_X(P) is again a perverse sheaf. The self‑duality is a key ingredient in the proof of the decomposition theorem because it forces the direct summands of Rf_* IC_X to be self‑dual up to shift, which characterises intersection complexes of subvarieties with semisimple local systems. On a stratified space X = ∪_α X_α, a perverse sheaf can be described by gluing data: for each stratum inclusion i_α: X_α → X, the costalk and stalk cohomology groups H^*(i_α^! P) and H^*(i_α^* P) satisfy support and cosupport conditions. The gluing formalism of MacPherson and Vilonen (1986) expresses the category of perverse sheaves on X as the category of diagrams of vector spaces attached to the strata, with linear maps given by the nearby and vanishing cycles along the inclusions of closures. This combinatorial description makes it possible to compute perverse sheaves on toric varieties, Schubert varieties, and nilpotent cones by reducing to quiver representations. Verdier duality acts on the diagram by reversing arrows and dualising vector spaces. The self‑duality of the perverse t‑structure implies that the category of perverse sheaves is a Frobenius category, and its stable category is equivalent to the derived category of constructible sheaves modulo the subcategory of complexes with zero perverse cohomology. This perspective underlies the geometric Satake correspondence, where the category of perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian Gr_G is identified with the category of representations of the Langlands dual group ^L G.

Geometric Langlands and the Role of Perverse Sheaves

The geometric Langlands program seeks a categorical equivalence between D‑modules on the moduli stack Bun_G of G‑bundles on a smooth projective curve X and coherent sheaves on the moduli stack LocSys^L G of local systems for the Langlands dual group ^L G. Perverse sheaves enter through the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence: regular holonomic D‑modules on Bun_G correspond to perverse sheaves on the associated analytic stack. The Hecke operators act on D‑modules on Bun_G by convolution with perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian Gr_G. The geometric Satake equivalence (Mirković–Vilonen, 2007) identifies the category PervG(O)(Gr_G) of G(O)‑equivariant perverse sheaves on Gr_G with the category Rep(^L G) of finite‑dimensional representations of ^L G. Under this equivalence, the convolution product corresponds to the tensor product of representations. A Hecke eigensheaf is a perverse sheaf (or D‑module) on Bun_G which is an eigenobject for all Hecke operators; its eigenvalues are given by a local system on X, i.e., a point of LocSys^L G. The work of Lafforgue (2002) for GL_n over function fields and of Gaitsgory, Lurie, and others for the categorical version over ℂ uses the theory of perverse sheaves on the moduli stack of shtukas and on the affine Grassmannian. The decomposition theorem guarantees that the pushforward of the constant sheaf along the Hitchin fibration h: M_H → A decomposes into a sum of intersection complexes of the fibers, which are Lagrangian subvarieties. This decomposition is the geometric counterpart of the spectral decomposition of the space of automorphic forms. The perverse Leray filtration on the cohomology of the Hitchin moduli space coincides with the weight filtration on the corresponding mixed Hodge modules, providing a bridge between the topological and Hodge‑theoretic aspects of the correspondence. Recent advances by Arinkin–Gaitsgory (2015) on the categorical geometric Langlands for GL_n use the theory of ind‑perverse sheaves on the Ran space to construct the required equivalence. The perverse t‑structure remains the central organising principle throughout these developments.

Computational Aspects: Algorithms for Intersection Cohomology and Perverse Sheaves

Effective computation of intersection cohomology groups and perverse sheaf cohomology has become feasible through algorithms implemented in computer algebra systems. The de Cataldo–Migliorini algorithm (2009) computes the decomposition of Rf_* IC_X for a projective morphism f: X → Y by reducing to the computation of the perverse Leray filtration on the cohomology of the fibers. For a toric variety X_Σ defined by a fan Σ, the intersection cohomology Betti numbers are given by the h‑vector of the associated polytope, which can be computed via the Stanley–Reisner ring of Σ. The software package “Perverse” for Macaulay2 (developed by M. Saito and collaborators) constructs the perverse sheaf associated to a given stratification by building the gluing diagram of vector spaces and linear maps. For Schubert varieties in the flag variety G/B, the Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials Pw,v(q) can be computed recursively using the Hecke algebra multiplication rules; the coefficients give the stalk dimensions of the intersection cohomology complexes ICX_w. The algorithm of Braden–MacPherson (1999) computes the intersection cohomology of a stratified space by a sequence of pushforwards and nearby cycles along a filtration by closed subvarieties; this algorithm has been implemented in the “IntersectionCohomology” package for SageMath. In practice, one often works with the Verdier dual of a perverse sheaf to obtain the costalk data, which is easier to compute because it involves only local cohomology with support. The complexity of these algorithms is polynomial in the number of strata and the Betti numbers of the links, but exponential in the dimension of the variety in the worst case. For exam purposes, it is sufficient to know that intersection cohomology of toric varieties is combinatorial, that Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials are computable via the Hecke algebra, and that the decomposition theorem can be checked on a case‑by‑case basis using the perverse Leray spectral sequence.

  • Confusing the weight filtration on mixed Hodge modules with the perverse Leray filtration; they coincide only after applying the forgetful functor to perverse sheaves.
  • Assuming the decomposition theorem holds for non‑proper morphisms; properness is essential for semisimplicity of the pushforward.
  • Neglecting the shift by dimension in the definition of IC_X = j!* ℚ_U[dim X]; forgetting the shift leads to incorrect Poincaré duality statements.
  • Treating Verdier duality as an equivalence of abelian categories on Perv(X) without the shift; D_X is an anti‑equivalence of the derived category but restricts to an equivalence Perv(X) ≅ Perv(X)^op only after accounting for the perverse t‑structure.
  • Misidentifying the geometric Satake category as all perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian; it is the subcategory of G(O)‑equivariant perverse sheaves.
  • Believing that the relative hard Lefschetz isomorphism holds for any ample line bundle on the total space; it requires relative ampleness over the base.
  • Overlooking the necessity of regular holonomicity in the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence; irregular D‑modules correspond to enhanced perverse sheaves, not ordinary constructible sheaves.

hand/chemical-equilibrium.html:
Temperature Dependence of the Equilibrium Constant and Van't Hoff Equation

The equilibrium constant is not truly constant; it varies with temperature because the standard Gibbs energy change ΔG° = −RT ln K depends on temperature through both the explicit T factor and the temperature dependence of ΔH° and ΔS°. For a reaction with a known standard enthalpy change ΔH°, the integrated Van't Hoff equation relates the equilibrium constants at two temperatures:

ln(K₂/K₁) = −ΔH°/R (1/T₂ − 1/T₁)

where R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. This expression assumes ΔH° is temperature‑independent over the interval, an approximation that holds well for modest temperature ranges. If ΔH° > 0 (endothermic), increasing T makes the term (1/T₂ − 1/T₁) negative, so ln(K₂/K₁) becomes positive and K increases. Conversely, for an exothermic reaction (ΔH° < 0) K decreases as temperature rises. The qualitative prediction matches Le Chatelier's principle: heat is a reactant in endothermic processes and a product in exothermic ones.

A Van't Hoff plot of ln K versus 1/T yields a straight line of slope −ΔH°/R and intercept ΔS°/R. Experimental determination of K at several temperatures therefore provides both ΔH° and ΔS° without calorimetry. In practice, the plot often curves because ΔH° itself varies with temperature (ΔCₚ ≠ 0). The curvature can be analysed using the Kirchhoff equation ΔH°(T₂) = ΔH°(T₁) + ∫ΔCₚ dT, but for most competitive‑exam problems the constant‑ΔH° approximation is sufficient.

Typical exam applications include the Haber synthesis (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH° = −92 kJ mol⁻¹). Raising the temperature from 400 °C to 500 °C reduces K dramatically, which is why industrial operation uses a compromise temperature (≈ 450 °C) together with high pressure to maintain reasonable yield. Another common question asks for the temperature at which K = 1; setting ln K = 0 in the integrated equation gives 1/T = 1/T₁ − (R/ΔH°) ln K₁.

Effect of Ionic Strength on Activity Coefficients and Apparent Equilibrium Constants

Thermodynamic equilibrium constants are defined in terms of activities aᵢ = γᵢ [Cᵢ], where γᵢ is the activity coefficient and [Cᵢ] the molar concentration. In dilute solutions γᵢ → 1 and the concentration‑based constant Kc approximates the true K. As ionic strength I = ½ Σ cᵢ zᵢ² increases, electrostatic interactions lower γᵢ below unity. The Debye–Hückel limiting law gives log₁₀ γᵢ = −A zᵢ² √I (A ≈ 0.509 mol⁻¹ᐟ² L¹ᐟ² at 25 °C). The extended Debye–Hückel equation adds a linear term in I to improve accuracy up to I ≈ 0.1 M.

Because each species carries its own γ, the apparent equilibrium constant expressed in concentrations, Kc′ = Π[products]ⁿ / Π[reactants]ᵐ, relates to the thermodynamic K by K = Kc′ × (Πγ_productsⁿ / Πγ_reactantsᵐ). For a reaction where the sum of product charges equals the sum of reactant charges, the γ‑ratio may be near unity even at moderate I, but for reactions that change the total charge (e.g., H⁺ + OH⁻ ⇌ H₂O) the effect is large. In buffer preparation, ignoring activity corrections can shift the pH by 0.1–0.3 units when the buffer concentration exceeds 0.1 M.

Practical calculations often use the Davies equation log₁₀ γ = −A z² (√I/(1+√I) − 0.3 I) for I up to 0.5 M. When solving equilibrium problems that involve added inert salts, first compute I from all ions present, then evaluate γ for each species, and finally solve the mass‑balance and charge‑balance equations using activities. This two‑step approach (estimate I, compute γ, iterate) is standard in rigorous analytical chemistry and appears in advanced competitive‑exam questions.

Van't Hoff Plot for Determining ΔH°
For the reaction N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) the equilibrium constant Kp is 6.8×10⁵ at 300 K and 1.2×10³ at 500 K. Assuming ΔH° is constant over this range, calculate ΔH° in kJ mol⁻¹.
Use the integrated Van't Hoff equation: ln(K₂/K₁) = −ΔH°/R (1/T₂ − 1/T₁).
K₁ = 6.8×10⁵ at T₁ = 300 K; K₂ = 1.2×10³ at T₂ = 500 K.
ln(K₂/K₁) = ln(1.2×10³ / 6.8×10⁵) = ln(1.7647×10⁻³) = −6.337.
1/T₂ − 1/T₁ = 1/500 − 1/300 = 0.002 − 0.003333 = −0.001333 K⁻¹.
−ΔH°/R = ln(K₂/K₁) / (1/T₂ − 1/T₁) = (−6.337) / (−0.001333) = 4754 K.
ΔH° = −4754 K × 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = −39 540 J mol⁻¹ ≈ −39.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
The negative sign confirms the reaction is exothermic, consistent with the known ΔH° ≈ −92 kJ mol⁻¹; the discrepancy arises because ΔH° is not strictly constant over a 200 K span.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the effect of temperature on K, first identify the sign of ΔH° from the reaction enthalpy or from the direction of K change with T. Use the qualitative Van't Hoff trend (K rises with T for endothermic, falls for exothermic) to eliminate wrong options before any calculation. If a numeric answer is required, write the integrated equation, substitute values with consistent units (K in Kelvin, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), and keep track of signs.

Polyprotic Acid–Base Equilibria and Stepwise Dissociation Constants

Polyprotic acids donate protons sequentially, each step characterised by its own equilibrium constant Ka₁, Ka₂, … . For a diprotic acid H₂A the equilibria are H₂A ⇌ H⁺ + HA⁻ (Ka₁) and HA⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + A²⁻ (Ka₂). Typically Ka₁ ≫ Ka₂ (often by 4–6 orders of magnitude) because removing a proton from a negatively charged species is harder. The overall dissociation constant for the reaction H₂A ⇌ 2H⁺ + A²⁻ is Ka₁·Ka₂. In pH calculations, the first dissociation usually dominates the H⁺ concentration; the second contributes appreciably only when Ka₁ is not overwhelmingly larger than Ka₂ or when the solution is very dilute.

For a solution of initial concentration C of H₂A, the exact charge‑balance equation is [H⁺] = [HA⁻] + 2[A²⁻] + [OH⁻]. Using the stepwise expressions [HA⁻] = Ka₁[H₂A]/[H⁺] and [A²⁻] = Ka₁Ka₂[H₂A]/[H⁺]², together with the mass balance C = [H₂A] + [HA⁻] + [A²⁻], yields a cubic in [H⁺]. The common approximation [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka₁C) works when Ka₁C ≫ Ka₂ and [H⁺] ≫ [OH⁻]. If Ka₁C is comparable to Ka₂, the full cubic or a numerical solver is required.

Amphiprotic species such as HA⁻ can act as either acid or base. Their pH in a solution of the pure amphiprotic salt (e.g., NaHA) is given by the average of the two pKa values: pH ≈ (pKa₁ + pKa₂)/2, provided the concentration is not extremely low. This result follows from setting [H₂A] = [A²⁻] in the equilibrium expressions. For phosphoric acid (pKa₁ = 2.15, pKa₂ = 7.20, pKa₃ = 12.35) the dihydrogen phosphate / hydrogen phosphate buffer (H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻) operates near pH 7.2, while the hydrogen phosphate / phosphate buffer (HPO₄²⁻/PO₄³⁻) works near pH 12.3. Each buffer region is centred on the corresponding pKa and is effective within ±1 pH unit.

Titration curves of polyprotic acids show multiple equivalence points. The first equivalence point occurs when one equivalent of base has been added per mole of H₂A; the pH at this point is determined by the hydrolysis of HA⁻. The second equivalence point corresponds to complete conversion to A²⁻. The half‑equivalence points (where added base equals half the moles needed for the next equivalence) give pH = pKa₁ and pH = pKa₂ respectively, providing experimental routes to determine the stepwise constants.

Solubility Product, Common Ion Effect, and Precipitation Calculations

The solubility product Ksp is the equilibrium constant for the dissolution of a sparingly soluble salt: MₓAᵧ(s) ⇌ x Mʸ⁺(aq) + y Aˣ⁻(aq). For a simple 1:1 salt such as AgCl, Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]. The molar solubility s (mol L⁻¹) in pure water satisfies s² = Ksp, so s = √Ksp. For a salt of type M₂A (e.g., Ag₂CrO₄) the dissolution gives 2Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻, and Ksp = (2s)²·s = 4s³, yielding s = (Ksp/4)¹ᐟ³.

The common ion effect states that adding a soluble salt sharing an ion with the sparingly soluble salt reduces its solubility. If a solution already contains [Cl⁻] = C from NaCl, the equilibrium condition becomes [Ag⁺] = Ksp / C, so the solubility of AgCl drops linearly with the common‑ion concentration. This principle underlies selective precipitation: by adjusting the concentration of a common ion, one can precipitate the less soluble salt while keeping the more soluble one in solution. For example, adding (NH₄)₂SO₄ to a mixture of Ba²⁺ and Sr²⁺ precipitates BaSO₄ (Ksp = 1.1×10⁻¹⁰) before SrSO₄ (Ksp = 3.2×10⁻⁷) because BaSO₄ requires a lower [SO₄²⁻] to exceed its Ksp.

pH strongly influences the solubility of salts of weak acids. For a salt MA where A⁻ is the conjugate base of a weak acid HA (Ka), the dissolution equilibrium couples with the acid‑base equilibrium A⁻ + H⁺ ⇌ HA. In acidic solution, the added H⁺ shifts this equilibrium to the right, consuming A⁻ and increasing the solubility. Quantitatively, the conditional solubility s' at a fixed [H⁺] satisfies Ksp = s'·[A⁻] where [A⁻] = s'·Ka/(Ka + [H⁺]). Solving gives s' = √(Ksp·(Ka + [H⁺])/Ka). This explains why CaCO₃ (Ksp = 3.3×10⁻⁹) dissolves readily in acid but is sparingly soluble in neutral water.

In mixed‑ion solutions, the ion product Q = [Mʸ⁺]ˣ[Aˣ⁻]ʸ is compared with Ksp. If Q > Ksp, precipitation occurs until Q = Ksp. The amount precipitated can be found by solving the simultaneous mass‑balance and equilibrium equations. Competitive‑exam problems often ask for the minimum concentration of a precipitating agent required to start precipitation of one ion while keeping another in solution, which is a direct application of the common‑ion and selective‑precipitation concepts.

Electrochemical Cells and the Nernst Equation at Equilibrium

The thermodynamic link between electrochemistry and chemical equilibrium is ΔG° = −nFE°cell = −RT ln K. For a generic redox reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the reaction quotient Q = ([C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ)/([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ). The Nernst equation gives the cell potential under non‑standard conditions: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q. At equilibrium E = 0 and Q = K, so 0 = E° − (RT/nF) ln K, which rearranges to ln K = nFE°/RT. This relationship allows calculation of K from standard electrode potentials, and vice versa.

For a concentration cell with identical electrodes but different ion activities, E° = 0 and the potential arises solely from the activity ratio: E = (RT/nF) ln (a₂/a₁). At 25 °C, RT/F = 0.025693 V, so for a one‑electron process E = 0.05916 log₁₀ (a₂/a₁). This principle is used in ion‑selective electrodes (e.g., the glass pH electrode) where the measured potential directly reports the activity of H⁺.

Temperature dependence of E° follows from the Gibbs‑Helmholtz relation: (∂(ΔG°/T)/∂T)ₚ = −ΔH°/T². Since ΔG° = −nFE°, one obtains (∂E°/∂T)ₚ = ΔS°/nF. In practice, standard potentials are tabulated at 298 K; for other temperatures the Van't Hoff approach using ΔH° and ΔS° derived from electrochemical data can be employed.

Applications in competitive exams include: (i) calculating K for the Daniell cell (Zn + Cu²⁺ ⇌ Zn²⁺ + Cu) from E° = 1.10 V, giving log₁₀ K = nE°/0.05916 ≈ 37.2, so K ≈ 1.6×10³⁷; (ii) determining the equilibrium constant for the disproportionation of Cu⁺ (2Cu⁺ ⇌ Cu²⁺ + Cu) using the two half‑reaction potentials; (iii) predicting the direction of spontaneous reaction by comparing Q with K via the sign of E. Mastery of the Nernst equation, the conversion between natural and base‑10 logarithms, and the use of activities rather than concentrations at high ionic strength are essential for full marks.

  • Assuming ΔH° is temperature‑independent when the problem explicitly states a large temperature range; the Van't Hoff plot will curve and the simple two‑point formula gives an average ΔH°, not the true value at either temperature.
  • Neglecting activity coefficients in Ksp or buffer calculations at ionic strengths above 0.01 M, leading to systematic errors in predicted solubility or pH.
  • Treating the second dissociation of a diprotic acid as independent of the first; the correct mass‑balance couples Ka₁ and Ka₂, and the approximation [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka₁C) fails when Ka₁C is not ≫ Ka₂.
  • Confusing the common‑ion effect on solubility with the common‑ion effect on a weak‑acid equilibrium; the former reduces solubility linearly with the added ion concentration, the latter shifts the acid dissociation according to Le Chatelier but does not change the total dissolved amount of the solid.
  • Using concentrations instead of activities in the Nernst equation for concentrated solutions; the potential then deviates from the ideal 0.05916 V per decade at 25 °C.
  • Forgetting that the half‑equivalence point of a polyprotic titration corresponds to pH = pKa only when the two successive pKa values are separated by at least 3 units; otherwise the buffer regions overlap and the simple relation breaks down.
  • Applying the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation to a buffer whose component ratio lies outside the 0.1–10 range; the buffer capacity is then too low and the equation no longer predicts the pH accurately.

These advanced topics extend the core equilibrium framework and are frequently tested in higher‑level chemistry examinations.

hand/math-logic.html:
Proof Theory and Ordinal Analysis

Proof theory studies formal proofs as mathematical objects, measuring the strength of theories by the ordinals needed to prove their consistency. Gentzen’s 1936 consistency proof for Peano Arithmetic (PA) uses transfinite induction up to the ordinal ε₀, the smallest ordinal satisfying ω^ε = ε. The proof proceeds by assigning to each derivation in PA an ordinal notation < ε₀ and showing that cut‑elimination reduces the ordinal, so an infinite descending sequence would contradict well‑foundedness of ε₀. This yields a finitary consistency proof relative to the principle of transfinite induction up to ε₀, which is not provable in PA itself (by Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem).

Subsequent work extended ordinal analysis to stronger systems. The Feferman–Schütte ordinal Γ₀ marks the limit of predicative analysis; theories such as ATR₀ (arithmetical transfinite recursion) have proof‑theoretic ordinal Γ₀. The Takeuti–Feferman–Buchholz ordinal analysis of Π¹₁‑CA₀ reaches the ordinal ψ(Ω_ω) in Buchholz’s ψ‑function. These ordinals are expressed using collapsing functions on large countable ordinals, providing a fine‑grained calibration of comprehension axioms. Ordinal analysis also connects to the slow‑growing and fast‑growing hierarchies: the provably total functions of a theory correspond exactly to those dominated by the fast‑growing hierarchy at its proof‑theoretic ordinal.

An examiner may ask to compare the proof‑theoretic strength of PA, ACA₀, and ATR₀. The correct ordering is PA < ACA₀ < ATR₀, with ordinals ε₀, ε₀, and Γ₀ respectively (ACA₀ is conservative over PA for arithmetical sentences, so it shares ε₀). A common trap is to claim ACA₀ has a larger ordinal because it includes arithmetical comprehension; the conservativity result shows otherwise.

Recursion Theory and the Structure of Turing Degrees

Recursion theory (now often called computability theory) classifies sets of natural numbers by their Turing degree, the equivalence class under Turing reducibility. The degree 0 consists of computable sets; 0′ (the jump of 0) is the degree of the halting problem. The jump operator A ↦ A′ is strictly increasing and defines the arithmetical hierarchy: Σ₁⁰ sets are exactly the 0‑r.e. sets, Π₁⁰ are co‑r.e., and Δ₁⁰ = 0. Post’s problem asked whether there exists an r.e. degree strictly between 0 and 0′. Friedberg and Muchnik (1956) independently solved it positively using the priority method, constructing an r.e. set of intermediate degree.

The priority method became the central tool for building degrees with prescribed properties. It yields results such as the existence of minimal degrees (degrees > 0 with no non‑zero degree below them), hyperimmune‑free degrees, and the Sacks Density Theorem: the r.e. degrees are dense. The global structure of the Turing degrees is an upper semilattice with least element 0 and a jump operation. The Turing degrees are not a lattice (Lachlan, 1966), and the first‑order theory of the degrees is undecidable (Simpson, 1977). The Martin conjecture (proved for uniformly invariant functions by Slaman and Steel) relates the Turing jump to the only natural order‑preserving functions on the degrees.

Examiners often test the distinction between many‑one reducibility (m‑reducibility) and Turing reducibility. Every m‑reduction is a Turing reduction, but the converse fails: there are sets A, B with A ≤_T B but not A ≤_m B. The Myhill isomorphism theorem states that A ≡_m B iff A and B are computably isomorphic. The Rice–Shapiro theorem characterises r.e. index sets: a property of r.e. sets is r.e. iff it is a union of basic open sets in the Scott topology.

Technique
Show that there exists an r.e. set A such that 0 <_T A <_T 0′. Outline the priority construction with requirements R_e: Φ_e^A ≠ K (where K is the halting set) and S_e: W_e ≠ A (where W_e is the e‑th r.e. set). Explain how injuries are resolved.
We build A in stages. At stage s we have a finite approximation A_s. For each requirement R_e we pick a witness x_e not yet used. We wait for Φ_eA_s(x_e) to converge; if it does, we enumerate x_e into A to make Φ_e^A(x_e) ≠ K(x_e). This may injure lower‑priority S_i requirements that had kept x_e out of A. For each S_e we pick a witness y_e and keep y_e out of A unless some higher‑priority R_i forces it in; if W_e eventually enumerates y_e, we change y_e to a fresh number. Because each requirement acts only finitely often (by the priority ordering), the construction yields an r.e. set A satisfying all R_e and S_e, hence 0 <_T A <_T 0′.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a degree construction, sketch the priority tree: list requirements in order, state the witness strategy, and argue finite injury. Do not write a full formal proof; a clear outline with the injury lemma earns full marks.

Forcing and Independence in Set Theory

Forcing, introduced by Paul Cohen in 1963, is a method for expanding a model of ZFC to a larger model in which a chosen statement fails, thereby proving its independence. A forcing notion (P, ≤) is a partially ordered set; a filter G ⊆ P is generic over a countable transitive model M if G meets every dense subset of P that belongs to M. The generic extension M[G] satisfies ZFC and the forcing relation ⊩ defines truth in M[G] by induction on formula complexity. Cohen’s original forcing adds a new subset of ω (a Cohen real), showing that the Continuum Hypothesis (CH) can fail while ZFC holds.

Subsequent forcing constructions established the independence of many combinatorial statements: Suslin’s Hypothesis (SH) is independent (Solovay–Tennenbaum, 1971); Martin’s Axiom (MA) plus ¬CH is consistent (Martin–Solovay, 1970); the Proper Forcing Axiom (PFA) implies 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₂ and settles many questions about Aronszajn trees. Iterated forcing with countable support preserves cardinals and allows the construction of models where the continuum is arbitrarily large (Easton’s theorem for regular cardinals). Large cardinal assumptions (measurable, supercompact) are used to obtain consistency of strong forcing axioms such as MM (Martin’s Maximum).

Examiners may ask to distinguish between product forcing and iteration. Product forcing adds many generics simultaneously and preserves chain conditions componentwise; iteration adds generics sequentially, and the choice of support (finite, countable, revised countable) determines which cardinals are preserved. A typical trap is to claim that adding a Cohen real preserves all cardinals — it preserves ℵ₁ but collapses 2^ℵ₀ to ℵ₁ in the ground model if CH held there.

Descriptive Set Theory and Determinacy

Descriptive set theory studies definable subsets of Polish spaces (e.g., ℝ, ω^ω). The Borel hierarchy Σ⁰_α, Π⁰_α, Δ⁰_α (α < ω₁) classifies sets by countable unions and intersections of open sets. The projective hierarchy Σ¹_n, Π¹_n, Δ¹_n is obtained by projecting Borel sets. Analytic sets (Σ¹1) are continuous images of Borel sets; co‑analytic sets (Π¹1) are their complements. The perfect set property holds for analytic sets: every uncountable analytic set contains a perfect subset.

Determinacy asserts that for a given pointclass Γ, every game G(A) with payoff set A ∈ Γ is determined (one player has a winning strategy). Gale–Stewart (1953) proved open games are determined. Martin (1975) proved Borel determinacy using a transfinite induction up to ω₁. Projective determinacy (PD) — determinacy for all projective sets — follows from the existence of infinitely many Woodin cardinals (Martin–Steel, 1989; Woodin, 1990s). PD implies regularity properties for projective sets: Lebesgue measurability, Baire property, and the perfect set property. The Axiom of Determinacy (AD) contradicts AC but holds in L(ℝ) under large cardinals.

A common exam question asks to prove that every Σ¹1 set has the perfect set property. The proof uses the fact that a Σ¹1 set is the projection of a closed set in ω^ω × ω^ω; if it is uncountable, a perfect subset can be extracted by a Cantor‑Bendixson analysis on the tree of the closed set. Another trap is to confuse analytic determinacy (provable in ZFC) with projective determinacy (requires large cardinals).

Finite Model Theory and Computational Complexity

Finite model theory investigates the expressive power of logics on finite structures, providing a logic‑based characterisation of complexity classes. Fagin’s theorem (1974) states that a property of finite structures is in NP iff it is definable in existential second‑order logic (∃SO). This yields a machine‑independent definition of NP. The logic FO(LFP) (first‑order logic with least fixed point) captures PTIME on ordered structures (Immerman–Vardi theorem, 1982). On unordered structures, FO(LFP) is strictly weaker; the Cai‑Fürer‑Immerman construction (1992) shows that fixed‑point logic with counting (FPC) still fails to capture PTIME.

Descriptive complexity also connects to the zero‑one law: for any first‑order sentence φ, the asymptotic probability that a random finite structure satisfies φ is either 0 or 1 (Glebskii et al., 1969; Fagin, 1976). This fails for logics with fixed‑point operators. Ehrenfeucht–Fraïssé games provide a combinatorial tool to prove inexpressibility: Duplicator has a winning strategy in the k‑round game on structures A and B iff A and B satisfy the same FO sentences of quantifier rank ≤ k. The number of rounds corresponds to the quantifier depth needed to distinguish the structures.

Examiners often test the distinction between ordered and unordered capture results. A typical question: “Does FO(LFP) capture PTIME on all finite structures?” The answer is no; it captures PTIME only on structures with a built‑in linear order (or at least a successor relation). Another trap is to assume that Fagin’s theorem gives a logical characterisation of P; it characterises NP, while P corresponds to FO(LFP) on ordered structures.

  • Confusing the proof‑theoretic ordinal of ACA₀ with that of PA — they are both ε₀ because ACA₀ is arithmetically conservative over PA.
  • Assuming every Turing reduction is a many‑one reduction; the Myhill isomorphism theorem only gives equivalence for computable isomorphisms.
  • Believing that adding a Cohen real preserves the continuum — it forces 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₁ in the extension, collapsing the ground model’s continuum if CH held.
  • Thinking Borel determinacy requires large cardinals — it is provable in ZFC via a transfinite induction up to ω₁.
  • Claiming FO(LFP) captures PTIME on unordered finite structures — the Cai‑Fürer‑Immerman counterexample shows it does not.
  • Mixing up the zero‑one law for FO with the behaviour of fixed‑point logics — the law fails for LFP and IFP.
  • Overlooking the role of the priority ordering in finite‑injury constructions — each requirement must be assigned a distinct priority to guarantee finite injury.

These advanced topics deepen the core material and are frequently targeted in higher‑level examinations.

hand/nuclear-chemistry.html:
Nuclear Shell Model and Magic Numbers

The nuclear shell model treats nucleons as moving independently in a mean‑field potential created by all other nucleons, analogous to the electronic shell model in atoms. The model successfully explains the exceptional stability of nuclei with certain numbers of protons or neutrons, known as magic numbers: 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, and 126. These numbers correspond to closed shells in the harmonic‑oscillator plus spin‑orbit potential. Nuclei with both proton and neutron magic numbers (doubly magic) such as 4He (Z=2, N=2), 16O (Z=8, N=8), 40Ca (Z=20, N=20), 48Ca (Z=20, N=28), 56Ni (Z=28, N=28), 100Sn (Z=50, N=50), 132Sn (Z=50, N=82) and 208Pb (Z=82, N=126) exhibit higher binding energies per nucleon, larger first excitation energies, and spherical ground‑state shapes.

The spin‑orbit term, introduced by Mayer and Jensen in 1949, splits each orbital angular momentum level into two sub‑levels (j = l ± ½) and is essential for reproducing the observed magic numbers beyond 20. The model also predicts the ordering of single‑particle levels, which governs the ground‑state spin and parity of odd‑A nuclei. For example, the ground state of 17O (Z=8, N=9) is 5/2+ because the extra neutron occupies the 1d5/2 orbital just above the closed N=8 shell.

Experimental verification comes from nuclear spectroscopy: magnetic moments, quadrupole moments, and excited‑state energies measured by γ‑ray spectroscopy, (d,p) transfer reactions, and Coulomb excitation. Deviations from the simple shell‑model predictions signal the onset of collective phenomena such as deformation, pairing correlations, and configuration mixing, which are treated in the interacting boson model and the deformed shell model (Nilsson model).

In astrophysics, the shell structure influences the r‑process path: nuclei near closed neutron shells (N=50, 82, 126) act as waiting points because their neutron‑capture cross sections are low and β‑decay half‑lives are relatively long, shaping the observed abundance peaks in the solar r‑process pattern.

Neutron Capture Processes: s‑process and r‑process

The slow neutron‑capture process (s‑process) occurs in thermally pulsing asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars where the neutron flux is modest (≈107 n cm−2 s−1) and the temperature is around 2–3 × 108 K. The main neutron source is the 13C(α,n)16O reaction during the interpulse period and the 22Ne(α,n)25Mg reaction during the thermal pulse. Because the neutron capture timescale is longer than typical β‑decay half‑lives, the reaction path follows the valley of stability, producing nuclei up to lead and bismuth. The s‑process is responsible for roughly half of the elements heavier than iron, with characteristic abundance peaks at magic neutron numbers N=50 (Sr, Y, Zr), N=82 (Ba, La, Ce) and N=126 (Pb, Bi).

The rapid neutron‑capture process (r‑process) requires an extreme neutron flux (>1022 n cm−2 s−1) and a short timescale (seconds). Candidate sites include core‑collapse supernovae (neutrino‑driven winds) and binary neutron‑star mergers, the latter strongly supported by the GW170817 kilonova observation. In the r‑process, neutron captures proceed far from stability until the neutron drip line is reached; subsequent β‑decays bring the material back to stability, creating the same magic‑number abundance peaks but shifted to heavier isotopes. The r‑process produces the heaviest naturally occurring elements, including thorium and uranium, and is the sole source of the actinides.

Both processes are sensitive to nuclear physics inputs: neutron‑capture cross sections, β‑decay half‑lives, nuclear masses, and fission barriers for the heaviest nuclei. Modern network calculations use experimentally measured rates where available and theoretical models (e.g., Hauser‑Feshbach for capture, QRPA for β‑decay) otherwise. The comparison of calculated abundance patterns with meteoritic and stellar spectroscopic data provides stringent tests of both astrophysical conditions and nuclear models.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which neutron‑capture process is responsible for the production of the majority of the solar system's lead isotopes?" The answer choices include s‑process, r‑process, p‑process, and α‑process.
The s‑process terminates at the lead‑bismuth region because the neutron capture cross sections of 204Pb, 206Pb, 207Pb and 208Pb are very small and the β‑decay of 209Bi (t1/2 ≈ 1.9 × 1019 yr) is effectively stable on astrophysical timescales. Consequently, the s‑process builds up lead isotopes and accounts for the bulk of solar lead. The r‑process also produces lead but its contribution is smaller and is accompanied by a large actinide inventory. Therefore the correct choice is the s‑process.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question contrasts s‑process and r‑process, first identify the neutron flux and timescale described. Low flux and long timescale → s‑process; high flux and short timescale → r‑process. Remember the key neutron sources (13C(α,n) and 22Ne(α,n) for s‑process) and the astrophysical sites (AGB stars vs. neutron‑star mergers). This quick classification eliminates two answer options instantly.

Radiation Detection and Measurement Techniques

Accurate detection of ionizing radiation relies on the interaction of radiation with matter. Gas‑filled detectors (ionization chambers, proportional counters, Geiger‑Müller tubes) collect charge pairs created by primary ionization. In an ionization chamber operated at low voltage, all ion pairs are collected, giving a current proportional to dose rate; these are used for absolute dosimetry. Proportional counters operate at higher voltage where gas amplification occurs, providing energy resolution sufficient for α‑particle spectroscopy (≈5 % FWHM at 5 MeV). Geiger‑Müller tubes operate in the Geiger region where each primary ionization triggers a full discharge, yielding high sensitivity but no energy discrimination.

Scintillation detectors convert radiation energy into visible photons. Inorganic crystals such as NaI(Tl) (thallium‑doped sodium iodide) offer high light yield and are standard for γ‑ray spectroscopy (resolution ≈7 % at 662 keV). High‑purity germanium (HPGe) detectors are semiconductor diodes cooled to liquid‑nitrogen temperature; they provide superior resolution (≈0.2 % at 1.33 MeV) and are essential for precise γ‑ray energy measurements in nuclear structure and environmental monitoring. Organic liquid scintillators (e.g., NE‑213) enable pulse‑shape discrimination between neutrons and γ‑rays, crucial for mixed‑field dosimetry.

Semiconductor detectors (Si(Li), Si PIN, CdTe, CZT) operate at room temperature (CdTe, CZT) or modest cooling (Si). They are compact, have fast response, and are used in X‑ray fluorescence, medical imaging (CdTe in CT), and space missions (CZT on the Swift Burst Alert Telescope). Solid‑state nuclear track detectors (CR‑39, LR‑115) record latent tracks from heavy charged particles; chemical etching reveals track density, providing integrated dose measurements for radon monitoring and cosmic‑ray studies.

Neutron detection exploits nuclear reactions with high cross sections: 3He(n,p)3H, 6Li(n,α)3H, 10B(n,α)7Li, and 235U(n,f). 3He proportional counters are the gold standard for thermal neutrons; however, 3He scarcity has driven development of 10B‑lined proportional tubes and 6Li‑glass scintillators. Fast neutrons are moderated before detection or measured via recoil protons in organic scintillators with pulse‑shape discrimination.

Nuclear Waste Management and Decommissioning

Radioactive waste is classified by activity level and half‑life: exempt waste (very low activity), very low‑level waste (VLLW), low‑level waste (LLW), intermediate‑level waste (ILW), and high‑level waste (HLW). HLW, primarily spent nuclear fuel and vitrified reprocessing waste, contains fission products (e.g., 90Sr, 137Cs) with half‑lives ~30 yr and actinides (Pu, Am, Cm) with half‑lives up to 105 yr. Heat generation from decay requires active cooling for decades.

Engineered barriers form the basis of geological disposal concepts. The waste form (borosilicate glass for HLW, cementitious grout for ILW) immobilizes radionuclides. The container (corrosion‑resistant steel or copper) provides mechanical integrity. The buffer (bentonite clay) limits water ingress and radionuclide migration. The host rock (granite, clay, salt, or tuff) provides long‑term isolation. Performance assessment models couple thermal, hydraulic, mechanical, and chemical (THMC) processes over timescales of 105–106 yr.

Decommissioning of nuclear facilities proceeds in three stages: immediate dismantling (DECON), safe enclosure (SAFSTOR) with deferred dismantling after 40–60 yr, and entombment (ENTOMB) where structures are encased in concrete. The choice depends on radiological inventory, regulatory framework, and funding. Characterisation surveys using in‑situ γ‑spectroscopy, neutron activation analysis, and core sampling guide segmentation and packaging of contaminated components. Waste minimisation techniques (chemical decontamination, melt‑refining of metals) reduce the volume of LLW/ILW requiring disposal.

International guidance is provided by the IAEA Safety Standards (e.g., GSR Part 5, WS‑R‑5) and the Joint Convention on the Safety of Spent Fuel Management and on the Safety of Radioactive Waste Management. National programmes (e.g., Finland’s Onkalo repository, Sweden’s SKB, France’s Cigéo) have advanced to licence application or construction phases, demonstrating the feasibility of deep geological disposal.

Advanced Radiometric Dating Methods: U‑Th, K‑Ar, and Cosmogenic Nuclides

Uranium‑thorium dating exploits the disequilibrium in the 238U decay series. 234U (t1/2 = 2.45 × 105 yr) decays to 230Th (t1/2 = 7.54 × 104 yr). In closed carbonate systems (corals, speleothems), the initial 230Th is negligible, and the 230Th/234U activity ratio grows with time, providing ages up to ~500 kyr with ±1 % precision. The method requires mass‑spectrometric measurement of isotope ratios (MC‑ICP‑MS) and correction for detrital 232Th using the 230Th/232Th ratio.

Potassium‑argon dating uses the electron‑capture decay of 40K (t1/2 = 1.248 × 109 yr) to 40Ar (10.7 % branching). The 40Ar/39Ar variant irradiates the sample to convert 39K to 39Ar, allowing simultaneous measurement of parent and daughter isotopes on a noble‑gas mass spectrometer. Step‑heating releases argon from different mineral domains, revealing thermal histories and excess argon. The technique dates volcanic rocks from a few thousand years to the age of the Earth.

Cosmogenic nuclide dating measures isotopes produced by cosmic‑ray interactions in surface rocks and sediments: 10Be (t1/2 = 1.39 × 106 yr), 26Al (t1/2 = 7.17 × 105 yr), 36Cl (t1/2 = 3.01 × 105 yr), and 14C (in quartz). Production rates depend on latitude, altitude, and shielding. The 26Al/10Be ratio is a powerful burial dating tool: when sediment is buried, production stops and the ratio decays with the differential half‑life, yielding burial ages up to ~5 Myr. These methods underpin studies of erosion rates, glacier chronologies, and landscape evolution.

  • Confusing the s‑process neutron source (13C(α,n)) with the r‑process site (neutron‑star merger) leads to wrong attribution of abundance peaks.
  • Assuming all γ‑ray detectors provide energy resolution; Geiger‑Müller tubes cannot discriminate energy.
  • Treating HLW heat load as negligible after a few years; actinide decay maintains significant heat for centuries.
  • Using 14C dating for samples older than 50 kyr where the signal is below detection limit.
  • Neglecting the need for detrital thorium correction in U‑Th dating of carbonates, which skews ages older.
  • Believing that all nuclear waste can be disposed of in a single repository design; waste classification dictates distinct engineered barriers.
  • Overlooking the role of pulse‑shape discrimination in organic scintillators for separating neutron and γ‑ray signals in mixed fields.
