hand/optimal-transport.html:
Regularity Theory for the Monge–Ampère Equation and Optimal Maps

The Brenier theorem guarantees that the optimal transport map between two absolutely continuous probability measures on ℝⁿ with quadratic cost is the gradient of a convex function φ solving the Monge–Ampère equation det D²φ(x) = ρ₀(x) / ρ₁(∇φ(x)). The regularity of φ — and hence of the transport map — is a central analytic question. Caffarelli’s interior regularity theory (1990‑1996) shows that if the source density ρ₀ and target density ρ₁ are bounded away from zero and infinity on convex domains, and the target domain is convex, then φ is strictly convex and belongs to C¹,α locally for some α∈(0,1). If, in addition, ρ₀ and ρ₁ are Ck,α and the domains are uniformly convex with Ck+2,α boundaries, then φ∈Ck+2,α up to the boundary. The global C¹,α estimate fails when the target domain is non‑convex; counterexamples by Caffarelli and McCann exhibit singular maps that concentrate mass on lower‑dimensional sets. The Alexandrov maximum principle and the Pogorelov estimate are the main tools: the former gives a pointwise bound on the Monge–Ampère measure of sections, the latter provides a second‑derivative bound in terms of the oscillation of φ. These results extend to Riemannian manifolds via the Ma–Trudinger–Wang (MTW) tensor; the MTW condition (non‑negative cross‑curvature) is necessary and sufficient for the continuity of optimal maps for the cost c(x,y)=½d(x,y)² on a compact manifold. In particular, on the sphere Sⁿ the MTW tensor is positive, yielding smooth optimal maps for smooth positive densities, while on the hyperbolic space it is negative, leading to possible discontinuities. The regularity theory also underpins the stability of optimal transport under perturbations of the marginals: if ρ₀^k→ρ₀ and ρ₁^k→ρ₁ in L¹, the corresponding optimal maps converge uniformly on compact subsets of the interior of the source domain, provided the uniform convexity and density bounds are preserved.

Entropic Regularization and the Sinkhorn Algorithm for Large‑Scale Wasserstein Computation

Computing the exact Wasserstein distance between discrete measures of size N requires solving a linear program with O(N³) complexity, which is prohibitive for N>10⁴. Entropic regularization replaces the Kantorovich problem by minimizing ∫ c dπ + ε H(π|μ⊗ν) over couplings π, where H is the relative entropy and ε>0 is a regularization parameter. The optimal coupling has the form πij=a_i Kij b_j with Kij=exp(−cij/ε). The scaling vectors a,b are obtained by the Sinkhorn iterations a←μ./(K b), b←ν./(Kᵀ a), which converge linearly to the unique solution. The regularized cost W2,ε²(μ,ν) converges to the true squared Wasserstein distance as ε→0, with an error of order ε log(1/ε) for smooth densities. In practice, ε is chosen as a trade‑off between bias and numerical stability; typical values are 10⁻²–10⁻¹ of the median pairwise cost. The algorithm can be accelerated by log‑domain stabilization, Anderson acceleration, or by using the Greenkhorn variant that updates only one coordinate per iteration. For continuous measures, the entropic problem admits a dual formulation involving the Schrödinger system ∂_t ρ_t = Δρ_t − ∇·(ρ_t ∇φ_t), ∂_t φ_t = −½|∇φ_t|² + εΔφ_t, linking optimal transport to the Schrödinger bridge problem. Recent work (Genevay, Peyré, Cuturi 2018) shows that the Sinkhorn divergence S_ε(μ,ν)=W2,ε²(μ,ν)−½W2,ε²(μ,μ)−½W2,ε²(ν,ν) defines a positive‑definite kernel on probability measures, enabling kernel methods in the Wasserstein space. The computational complexity of Sinkhorn is O(N²) per iteration, but low‑rank approximations of the kernel matrix (Nyström, random Fourier features) reduce it to O(N r) with r≪N, making it feasible for datasets of size 10⁵–10⁶.

Worked Example: Sinkhorn Iteration for Two Gaussian Mixtures
Let μ = 0.5 N(−2,1) + 0.5 N(2,1) and ν = 0.5 N(−1,1) + 0.5 N(1,1) be one‑dimensional Gaussian mixtures discretized on a uniform grid of 200 points covering [−6,6]. Take ε = 0.05. Perform three Sinkhorn iterations starting from a = 1, b = 1 and report the approximate transport plan mass on the diagonal entries (i=j).
1. Build cost matrix Cij = (x_i − y_j)². 2. Compute kernel Kij = exp(−Cij/ε). 3. Initialize a_i = 1, b_j = 1. 4. Iterate: a ← μ ./ (K b), b ← ν ./ (Kᵀ a). After three iterations the scaling vectors stabilize to a≈[0.98,…,1.02], b≈[1.01,…,0.99]. The diagonal of the coupling π = diag(a) K diag(b) carries about 0.62 of the total mass, reflecting the strong overlap of the mixture components. The regularized Wasserstein distance squared is ∑i,j πij Cij ≈ 1.03, while the exact W₂² between the mixtures is 1.00. The bias ≈0.03 is consistent with the ε log(1/ε) estimate.
Exam‑Day Strategy for Entropic OT Questions
When a question asks for the effect of ε on the Sinkhorn approximation, remember: (i) the regularized distance is always ≥ the true distance; (ii) the bias decays like ε log(1/ε) for smooth densities; (iii) too small ε causes numerical underflow in K — use log‑domain updates. If asked to compare Sinkhorn divergence with the raw regularized cost, note that the divergence removes the self‑regularization bias and yields a metric‑like quantity. Memorize the dual Schrödinger system; it frequently appears in questions linking OT to diffusion processes.

Mean‑Field Games and Gradient Flows in the Wasserstein Space

The connection between optimal transport and mean‑field games (MFG) was established by Lasry and Lions (2006‑2007). An MFG describes a continuum of identical agents whose state distribution ρ_t evolves according to a controlled continuity equation ∂_t ρ_t + ∇·(ρ_t α_t) = 0, where the control α_t = −∇u_t is derived from a value function u_t solving the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation −∂_t u_t + ½|∇u_t|² = f(x,ρ_t) with terminal condition u_T = g(x,ρ_T). The pair (ρ_t,u_t) satisfies the MFG system, which can be interpreted as the optimality conditions for the variational problem infρ,α ∫₀^T ∫ [½|α|² + F(x,ρ)] ρ dx dt + ∫ G(x,ρ_T) dx, where F = ∫₀^ρ f(x,s) ds and G = ∫₀^ρ g(x,s) ds. This is precisely a gradient flow of the energy ℰ(ρ)=∫ F(x,ρ) dx + ∫ G(x,ρ) dx in the Wasserstein space, with the Hamiltonian H(ρ,∇u)=∫ ½|∇u|² ρ dx. The JKO scheme (Jordan–Kinderlehrer–Otto 1998) provides a time‑discretization: ρk+1 = argmin_ρ [ (1/2τ) W₂²(ρ,ρ_k) + ℰ(ρ) ]. For the Boltzmann entropy ℰ(ρ)=∫ ρ log ρ dx, the JKO step recovers the heat equation ∂_t ρ = Δρ as the gradient flow of entropy in (P₂,W₂). More generally, for ℰ(ρ)=∫ V ρ dx + ∫ U(ρ) dx with convex U, the gradient flow is the nonlinear diffusion ∂_t ρ = ∇·(ρ ∇(V + U'(ρ))). The displacement convexity of ℰ along Wasserstein geodesics (McCann 1997) guarantees exponential convergence to equilibrium when the potential V is λ‑convex, with rate λ. This framework extends to interaction energies ℰ(ρ)=½∫∫ W(x−y) dρ(x) dρ(y), yielding the aggregation equation ∂_t ρ = ∇·(ρ ∇(W*ρ)). The well‑posedness theory for MFGs in the Wasserstein space relies on the monotonicity of the coupling f(x,ρ) (Lasry–Lions monotonicity condition) and on the convexity of the Hamiltonian in the momentum variable. Recent developments (Cardaliaguet, Delarue, Lasry, Lions 2019) establish a master equation on the space of measures, whose solution provides a feedback law for the N‑player game as N→∞.

Quantitative Stability of Optimal Transport Maps under Marginal Perturbations

Stability estimates quantify how much the optimal map T changes when the source μ or target ν is perturbed. For quadratic cost on ℝⁿ, if μ,ν have densities bounded below by c>0 and above by C<∞ on convex domains, and the target domain is uniformly convex, then the optimal map T is C¹,α and satisfies a Lipschitz stability bound: ‖Tμ,ν − Tμ',ν'‖L^∞(K) ≤ C_K ( W₁(μ,μ') + W₁(ν,ν') ) for any compact K⊂int(supp μ). The constant C_K depends on the density bounds, the convexity modulus of the target domain, and the distance of K to the boundary. This result follows from the Caffarelli contraction principle: the optimal map is 1‑Lipschitz when the target density is log‑concave and the source is uniform on a convex set. For general densities, the map is the gradient of a convex function φ solving the Monge–Ampère equation; stability of viscosity solutions yields the estimate. In the discrete setting, if μ_N, ν_N are empirical measures of N i.i.d. samples from μ,ν, then with high probability W₂(μ_N,μ) ≤ C N−1/n (up to log factors). Consequently, the empirical optimal map T_N converges uniformly to T at rate N−1/n on compact subsets. For entropic regularization, the Sinkhorn map T_ε satisfies ‖T_ε − T‖L²(μ) ≤ C √ε |log ε| under the same regularity assumptions. These quantitative bounds are essential for statistical applications: they guarantee that plug‑in estimators of the Wasserstein distance or of the optimal map are consistent and admit central limit theorems when n=1 (where the optimal map is the monotone rearrangement) or when the target is a Gaussian (where the map is affine). The theory also extends to the multi‑marginal problem, where stability of the multi‑marginal plan under perturbations of each marginal is controlled by the sum of the individual Wasserstein distances.

Martingale Optimal Transport and its Role in Model‑Free Finance

Martingale optimal transport (MOT) adds a martingale constraint to the Kantorovich problem: the coupling π must satisfy ∫ y π_x(dy) = x for μ‑a.e. x, where π_x is the disintegration of π with respect to its first marginal. This constraint encodes the no‑arbitrage condition in financial mathematics: the price process of a tradable asset under a risk‑neutral measure is a martingale. The MOT problem was introduced by Beiglböck, Henry‑Labordère, and Penkner (2013) and independently by Galichon, Henry‑Labordère, and Touzi (2014). The dual formulation involves functions φ,ψ and a process H adapted to the filtration such that φ(x)+ψ(y)+H(x)(y−x) ≥ c(x,y). The optimizer is characterized by a monotonicity principle: the support of the optimal coupling is contained in a set where the martingale condition holds with equality for a suitable “shadow” measure. For the quadratic cost c(x,y)=|x−y|², the optimal MOT coupling between two centered measures μ≺_c ν (convex order) is given by the left‑curtain coupling of Henry‑Labordère and Touzi (2016), which can be constructed via a monotone rearrangement of the quantile functions. The MOT cost provides model‑free bounds on exotic option prices: the supremum of E[Φ(S_T)] over all martingale laws with given marginals μ_t equals the MOT cost with cost Φ. This yields robust super‑replication prices without specifying a volatility model. Numerically, MOT can be solved by a variant of the Sinkhorn algorithm that enforces the martingale constraint via a penalization term λ‖∫ y π_x(dy) − x‖², or by a linear programming formulation on a grid with the martingale constraints as linear equalities. The theory extends to multi‑period MOT, where the coupling is a martingale measure on a product space, and to the computation of the Wasserstein distance between martingale laws (the adapted Wasserstein distance of Backhoff‑Veraguas, Beiglböck, and Pammer 2020).

  • Confusing the Monge map (deterministic) with the Kantorovich plan (probabilistic) when the source measure has atoms — the Monge problem may have no solution while the Kantorovich problem always does.
  • Assuming Caffarelli’s global regularity holds for non‑convex target domains; counterexamples show singularities can appear even with smooth positive densities.
  • Treating the Sinkhorn divergence as a true metric — it is only a divergence; the triangle inequality fails for finite ε.
  • Neglecting the log‑domain stabilization in Sinkhorn iterations for small ε, leading to underflow and NaN values in practical code.
  • Applying the JKO scheme to energies that are not displacement convex without checking the λ‑convexity condition; the scheme may not converge to the intended gradient flow.
  • Overlooking the convex order requirement μ≺_c ν in martingale optimal transport; without it the MOT problem is infeasible.
  • Confusing the adapted Wasserstein distance (which respects the filtration) with the standard Wasserstein distance when evaluating multi‑period model‑free bounds.

hand/heegaard-floer.html:
The Ozsváth-Szabó Spectral Sequence and Khovanov Homology

The Ozsváth-Szabó spectral sequence, constructed in 2005, provides a direct link between Khovanov homology (a combinatorial invariant of knots in S³) and the Heegaard Floer homology of the double cover of S³ branched along the knot. For a knot K ⊂ S³, let Σ(K) denote the double cover branched over K. There is a spectral sequence whose E² page is the reduced Khovanov homology Kh(K) (with coefficients in F₂) and which converges to the Heegaard Floer homology HF⁻(Σ(K)) (also with F₂ coefficients). The differentials on the Eʳ pages are induced by counting holomorphic disks in a Heegaard diagram for Σ(K) that are adapted to the branched covering structure. This spectral sequence is functorial under knot cobordisms and respects the gradings: the homological grading in Khovanov homology corresponds to the Maslov grading in Heegaard Floer homology, while the quantum grading corresponds to the Alexander grading shifted by the signature of the knot. A key consequence is that the rank of HF⁻(Σ(K)) is bounded above by the rank of Kh(K). For alternating knots, the spectral sequence collapses at the E² page, giving an isomorphism Kh(K) ≅ HF⁻(Σ(K)). This collapse also holds for quasi-alternating knots, a class introduced by Manolescu and Ozsváth that includes all alternating knots and is closed under certain operations. The spectral sequence has been used to prove that Khovanov homology detects the unknot (Kronheimer-Mrowka) and to study the relationship between the slice genus and the Rasmussen invariant s(K). The construction uses a cube of resolutions of the knot diagram, where each vertex corresponds to a Heegaard diagram for a resolution of the knot, and the edges correspond to holomorphic disks that implement the Khovanov differential. The analysis of the moduli spaces of these disks is highly technical but yields a purely combinatorial description of the E² page and the higher differentials in terms of the knot diagram.

Bordered Heegaard Floer Homology and the Pairing Theorem

Bordered Heegaard Floer homology, developed by Lipshitz, Ozsváth, and Thurston (2008–2015), extends Heegaard Floer homology to 3-manifolds with boundary. A bordered 3-manifold is a compact oriented 3-manifold Y with a parametrized boundary ∂Y ≅ F(g, k), where F(g, k) is a genus g surface with k boundary components, equipped with a fixed diffeomorphism to a standard model. The invariant assigns to each bordered manifold a module over a differential graded algebra A(F) associated to the boundary surface. There are two types of modules: type D structures (right modules) and type A structures (left modules), which are dual to each other. The algebra A(F) is generated by Reeb chords on the boundary and has a combinatorial description in terms of strand diagrams. The pairing theorem states that if Y₁ and Y₂ are bordered manifolds with boundaries identified by an orientation-reversing diffeomorphism, then the Heegaard Floer homology of the closed manifold Y₁ ∪ Y₂ is given by the derived tensor product (or box tensor product) of the corresponding modules: CF⁻(Y₁ ∪ Y₂) ≃ CFA⁻(Y₁) ⊠ CFD⁻(Y₂). This theorem reduces the computation of Heegaard Floer homology for arbitrary 3-manifolds to the computation of bordered invariants for elementary building blocks (e.g., handlebodies, mapping cylinders of mapping class group elements). The bordered theory also provides a framework for understanding the surgery exact triangle and the mapping cone formula for rational surgeries. In particular, the bordered invariant of a solid torus with a given framing encodes the knot Floer homology of the core knot, and the pairing theorem recovers the surgery formula. The theory has been implemented in computer programs (e.g., the bordered package in Sage) and has enabled the computation of Heegaard Floer homology for all 3-manifolds with up to a certain complexity. The bordered theory also has a version for sutured manifolds (Juhász), which further generalizes the invariant to manifolds with boundary equipped with a suture.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "The Ozsváth-Szabó spectral sequence converges from Khovanov homology to which Heegaard Floer homology group?" A common mistake is to answer HF⁺ or HF̂. The correct target is HF⁻(Σ(K)) with F₂ coefficients. Another trap: the spectral sequence is only defined for knots in S³, not for links or knots in other 3-manifolds (though there are generalizations).
The Ozsváth-Szabó spectral sequence has E² page equal to the reduced Khovanov homology Kh(K) over F₂ and converges to HF⁻(Σ(K); F₂). The differentials are induced by holomorphic disks in a Heegaard diagram for the branched double cover. For alternating knots, the sequence collapses at E², giving an isomorphism. The target is specifically HF⁻, not HF⁺ or HF̂, because the construction uses the U-action and the minus version is the one that naturally appears from the cube of resolutions.
Exam-day strategy
When asked about the Ozsváth-Szabó spectral sequence, always specify the coefficients (F₂), the source (reduced Khovanov homology), and the target (HF⁻ of the branched double cover). Remember that the collapse for alternating/quasi-alternating knots is a key computational tool. For bordered Floer, recall the pairing theorem: CFA ⊠ CFD computes the closed manifold invariant. Know the two module types and that the algebra is generated by Reeb chords. These are standard facts that appear in written exams and oral defenses.

The Surgery Exact Triangle and the Mapping Cone Formula for Rational Surgeries

The surgery exact triangle in Heegaard Floer homology relates the invariants of three manifolds obtained by Dehn surgeries on a knot with slopes differing by 1. For a knot K ⊂ Y and a rational number r = p/q, let Y_r(K) denote the result of r-surgery. The exact triangle takes the form: … → HF⁻(Y) → HF⁻(Y_p/q(K)) → HF⁻(Y_(p-q)/q(K)) → … . This triangle holds for all flavors of Heegaard Floer homology (̂, ⁻, ⁺, ∞) and is a consequence of the fact that the three surgeries correspond to three different ways of filling a bordered manifold (the knot complement). The mapping cone formula, due to Ozsváth and Szabó (2003) for integer surgeries and extended by Ozsváth-Szabó-Thurston (2015) and others to rational surgeries, gives an explicit chain complex for HF⁻(Y_p/q(K)) in terms of the knot Floer complex CFK⁻(K). For integer surgery n, the complex is the mapping cone of a chain map v + h between two copies of the knot Floer complex, where v and h are the vertical and horizontal maps in the knot Floer complex (counting disks that pass through the basepoints w and z). For rational surgery p/q, the formula involves a more complicated mapping cone built from the knot Floer complex and the continued fraction expansion of p/q. The mapping cone formula has been used to compute Heegaard Floer homology of all surgeries on a knot, to prove the Property P theorem (non-trivial knots have no surgery yielding a homotopy sphere), and to study the L-space property of surgeries. In particular, a rational homology sphere Y is an L-space if and only if for every knot K ⊂ Y, the knot Floer complex satisfies certain rank conditions. The surgery exact triangle and mapping cone formula are also central to the proof of the L-space conjecture for graph manifolds and to the study of the knot concordance invariants τ and ν.

Involutive Heegaard Floer Homology and Correction Terms

Involutive Heegaard Floer homology, introduced by Hendricks, Manolescu, and Zemke (2017), refines Heegaard Floer homology by incorporating the conjugation symmetry on the Heegaard diagram. For a closed 3-manifold Y with a spinc structure s, the conjugation action on the Heegaard diagram induces a chain map ι on the Heegaard Floer complex CF⁻(Y, s) that squares to the identity up to chain homotopy. The involutive complex CFI⁻(Y, s) is the mapping cone of ι + id, and its homology HFI⁻(Y, s) is the involutive Heegaard Floer homology. This invariant carries more information than the ordinary Heegaard Floer homology; for example, it can distinguish some homology spheres that have isomorphic HF⁻. The involutive correction terms d̲(Y, s) and d̄(Y, s) are defined as the minimal gradings of non-torsion elements in the image of the map from HFI⁻ to HF⁻ and in the cokernel, respectively. These correction terms satisfy d̲ ≤ d ≤ d̄, where d is the ordinary Ozsváth-Szabó correction term (the minimal grading of a non-torsion element in HF⁻). For an L-space, d̲ = d = d̄. The involutive correction terms provide obstructions to a 3-manifold bounding a smooth 4-manifold with certain intersection forms, refining the classic Furuta-Ohta and Ozsváth-Szabó bounds. They also give constraints on the existence of metrics of positive scalar curvature and on the topology of 4-manifolds with boundary. The involutive theory has a bordered version and a knot version, leading to involutive knot Floer homology and new concordance invariants. The computation of HFI⁻ for Seifert fibered spaces and for surgeries on knots has been carried out using the mapping cone formula and the bordered theory.

The Isomorphism with Seiberg-Witten Floer Homology

The isomorphism between Heegaard Floer homology and Seiberg-Witten Floer homology is a landmark result proved independently by two groups: Kutluhan, Lee, and Taubes (2010–2020) and Colin, Ghiggini, and Honda (2011–2012). For a closed, oriented 3-manifold Y with a spinc structure s, there is a canonical isomorphism HF⁻(Y, s) ≅ HMW⁻(Y, s) (and similarly for the other flavors), where HMW⁻ denotes the Seiberg-Witten Floer homology (also called monopole Floer homology). The proof proceeds by constructing a sequence of correspondences between the two theories: Heegaard Floer homology is isomorphic to embedded contact homology (ECH) via the work of Taubes (ECH = HF⁺), and ECH is isomorphic to Seiberg-Witten Floer homology via the work of Taubes (SW = ECH). The combined isomorphism is often referred to as the "triangulation" of Floer homologies. The isomorphism respects the grading, the U-action, the contact invariant, and the surgery exact triangles. It implies that all the applications of Heegaard Floer homology (e.g., the Property P theorem, the L-space conjecture, the genus bound for knots) can be translated into the language of Seiberg-Witten theory, and vice versa. The isomorphism also provides a conceptual explanation for the symmetry properties of Heegaard Floer homology (e.g., the conjugation symmetry corresponds to the orientation reversal of the 3-manifold). The proof is highly analytic, involving the study of the Seiberg-Witten equations on the symplectization of a contact manifold and the compactification of the moduli spaces of solutions. The isomorphism has been extended to manifolds with boundary (bordered Heegaard Floer homology vs. bordered ECH) and to knots (knot Floer homology vs. sutured monopole Floer homology). This equivalence is considered one of the most important results in low-dimensional topology in the 21st century, unifying two a priori very different approaches to 3-manifold invariants.

  • Confusing the target of the Ozsváth-Szabó spectral sequence: it converges to HF⁻ of the branched double cover, not HF⁺ or HF̂.
  • Assuming the spectral sequence exists for links or knots in arbitrary 3-manifolds; it is originally defined only for knots in S³.
  • Misstating the pairing theorem: the box tensor product is CFA ⊠ CFD, not CFD ⊠ CFA (order matters because one is a left module and the other a right module).
  • Forgetting that the mapping cone formula for rational surgeries requires the continued fraction expansion of the surgery coefficient and is more complicated than the integer surgery formula.
  • Thinking that involutive correction terms d̲ and d̄ are always equal to the ordinary correction term d; they satisfy d̲ ≤ d ≤ d̄ and can be strictly different.
  • Believing the isomorphism with Seiberg-Witten Floer homology is a formal consequence of the definitions; it is a deep analytic theorem requiring the equivalence of three distinct theories (Heegaard Floer, ECH, SW).
  • Overlooking that the contact invariant c(ξ) lives in HF̂(−Y), not in HF⁻(Y), and that it vanishes for overtwisted contact structures but is non-zero for tight ones.

hand/probabilistic-method.html:
The Rödl Nibble and the Semi-Random Method

The Rödl nibble, introduced by Vojtěch Rödl in 1985, is a semi‑random technique for constructing large combinatorial structures such as Steiner systems, packings, and coverings. Unlike a purely random greedy algorithm, the nibble proceeds in rounds: in each round a random subset of the available objects is selected with a carefully tuned probability, then all objects that conflict with the chosen ones are removed. The process repeats until the pool is exhausted. The key insight is that by keeping the selection probability small — typically of order 1/Δ where Δ is the maximum degree of the conflict hypergraph — the dependencies between chosen objects remain weak enough that standard concentration inequalities (Chernoff bounds, Azuma’s inequality) guarantee the process stays close to its expected trajectory.

Formally, let H be a k‑uniform hypergraph on vertex set V with maximum degree Δ. We wish to find a large matching (a set of disjoint edges). The nibble chooses each edge independently with probability p = c/Δ for a suitable constant c < 1. After the first round, the expected number of chosen edges is p|E|, and the expected number of vertices covered is kp|E|. Because each vertex lies in at most Δ edges, the expected number of conflicts (edges sharing a vertex with a chosen edge) is at most kΔp|E| = ck|E|. By choosing c small enough, the fraction of edges removed is strictly less than 1, so a positive proportion of edges survives. Repeating the round on the surviving hypergraph yields a matching of size (1−o(1))|V|/k, which is asymptotically optimal for many designs.

The semi‑random method extends the nibble by allowing a limited amount of deterministic “cleaning” after each random round. For example, after a nibble round one may greedily add any remaining edges that do not conflict with the current matching, then delete all edges incident to the newly added ones. This hybrid approach often improves the constant factors and simplifies the analysis because the deterministic step eliminates the need to track very small residual degrees. The method has been pivotal in proving the existence of approximate Steiner systems (Rödl 1985), the existence of near‑optimal packings in hypergraphs (Frankl–Rödl 1987), and the construction of Ramsey graphs with improved bounds (Kim 1995).

Analytically, the nibble is usually studied via the differential equation method (Wormald). One defines state variables such as the number of uncovered vertices of each degree, writes the expected one‑step changes, and shows that the random process concentrates around the solution of the corresponding system of differential equations. The concentration follows from Azuma’s inequality applied to the vertex‑exposure martingale, with bounded differences because each round changes the degree of any vertex by at most k. The resulting theorem states that with high probability the nibble produces a matching covering all but o(|V|) vertices, and the number of rounds needed is O(log Δ). This quantitative control makes the nibble a versatile tool for algorithmic applications, including polynomial‑time algorithms for finding large matchings in hypergraphs with bounded degree.

The Container Method for Independent Sets and Hypergraph Matchings

The container method, developed independently by Balogh, Morris, and Samotij (2015) and by Saxton and Thomason (2015), provides a powerful framework for counting and extremal problems in sparse graphs and hypergraphs. The central idea is to show that every independent set (or more generally, every set avoiding a fixed family of “bad” configurations) is contained in one of a relatively small collection of “containers”, each of which is itself nearly independent. Once such a container family is constructed, many counting and extremal questions reduce to analyzing the containers, which are far fewer than the independent sets themselves.

Let H be a k‑uniform hypergraph on n vertices with average degree d. The container lemma asserts that there exists a family C of subsets of V(H) such that: (1) every independent set of H is a subset of some C ∈ C; (2) each container C has size at most (1−δ)n for some δ = δ(k, d/n) > 0; (3) the number of containers is at most exp(O(n/d1/(k−1))). The proof uses an iterative “supersaturation” argument: if a set U is large, it contains many edges of H; one then selects a small “fingerprint” of vertices from U that determines a container containing U. The fingerprint size is bounded by a function of the codegree conditions, and the number of possible fingerprints yields the bound on |C|.

Applications are numerous. For the number of independent sets in a graph G with maximum degree Δ, the container method gives the sharp bound i(G) ≤ exp(O(n log Δ / Δ)), matching the known lower bound from disjoint unions of cliques. In hypergraph Ramsey theory, containers yield the best known upper bounds for the number of H‑free graphs and for the size of the largest H‑free subgraph of a random graph G(n,p). The method also gives a new proof of the Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem for intersecting families and provides a unified approach to the problem of counting proper colourings of graphs.

Algorithmic versions of the container lemma have been developed, allowing one to enumerate all independent sets in time proportional to the number of containers. This has led to fixed‑parameter tractable algorithms for counting independent sets in graphs of bounded degree and for sampling independent sets from the hard‑core model at low fugacity. The container method thus bridges extremal combinatorics, probabilistic combinatorics, and theoretical computer science.

Worked Example: Applying the Container Lemma to Count Independent Sets in a 3‑Regular Graph
Let G be a 3‑regular graph on n vertices. Use the container method to show that the number of independent sets i(G) is at most exp(O(n log 3 / 3)). Outline the main steps and give the final asymptotic bound.

Step 1: View independent sets of G as independent sets in the 2‑uniform hypergraph H = G (edges are the edges of G). Here k = 2, average degree d = 3.

Step 2: Apply the container lemma for graphs (k = 2). There exists a family C of subsets of V(G) such that every independent set I ⊆ V(G) is contained in some C ∈ C, each C has size at most (1−δ)n with δ = c/d for some absolute constant c > 0, and |C| ≤ exp(O(n/d)) = exp(O(n/3)).

Step 3: For each container C, the number of independent sets inside C is at most 2|C| ≤ 2(1−δ)n. Summing over all containers gives i(G) ≤ |C|·2(1−δ)n ≤ exp(O(n/3))·2(1−δ)n = exp(O(n log 2 / 3) + O(n/3)) = exp(O(n log 3 / 3)) because log 3 ≈ 1.585 and log 2 ≈ 0.693, and the dominant term is O(n log 3 / 3).

Thus i(G) ≤ exp(O(n log 3 / 3)), which matches the known bound up to the constant in the exponent.

Exam Strategy
When a question asks for an asymptotic bound on the number of independent sets or H‑free subgraphs, first identify the uniformity k and the average degree d of the relevant hypergraph. Then recall the container lemma’s three guarantees: containment, size reduction, and number of containers. Combine the container count with the trivial bound 2|C| for each container. The exponent will typically be O(n log d / d) for graphs and O(n / d1/(k−1)) for k‑uniform hypergraphs. Practice writing the three‑step outline; it earns full credit even if the constant factors are not fully optimized.

Entropy Compression and Algorithmic Extensions of the Lovász Local Lemma

Entropy compression, introduced by Moser and Tardos (2010) as part of their algorithmic proof of the Lovász Local Lemma (LLL), has evolved into a general method for analyzing randomized algorithms that repeatedly resample variables to avoid bad events. The core idea is to encode the execution log of the algorithm into a compressed string whose length is bounded by the entropy of the random bits used. If the algorithm runs for too many steps, the compression would violate the entropy bound, forcing termination. This technique yields not only expected polynomial running time but also strong tail bounds on the number of resampling steps.

In the variable model, each bad event A_i is determined by a subset of independent random variables. The Moser–Tardos algorithm starts with a random assignment, then while some A_i occurs, it resamples all variables that determine A_i. The analysis builds a witness tree for each resampling step: a rooted tree where nodes correspond to resampled events, edges represent dependency, and the tree structure captures the causal history. The probability that a given witness tree appears is at most the product of the probabilities of its nodes. Summing over all possible trees and using the LLL condition (ep(d+1) ≤ 1) shows that the expected number of resamplings is at most ∑ x_i/(1−x_i), where x_i are the LLL weights.

Entropy compression refines this by assigning a unique “compressed” description to each possible execution. One records the sequence of resampled events and the random bits used for each resampling. Because the LLL condition guarantees that the number of possible witness trees of a given size grows slower than the entropy of the random bits, the description length is strictly less than the number of random bits consumed, unless the algorithm terminates quickly. This yields a deterministic bound: with probability at least 1−2−Ω(t), the algorithm terminates after at most t resampling steps.

Beyond the LLL, entropy compression has been applied to graph colouring (the “naïve” algorithm for (Δ+1)‑colouring), to the construction of non‑repetitive sequences, and to the analysis of the “random greedy” algorithm for independent sets in hypergraphs. In each case, the method replaces a delicate probabilistic argument with a clean information‑theoretic counting argument. The technique also connects to the “partial rejection sampling” framework of Guo, Jerrum, and Liu (2019), which provides a unified algorithmic LLL for arbitrary product distributions.

The Probabilistic Method in Ramsey Theory: Lower Bounds and Explicit Constructions

Ramsey theory asks for the minimum N such that any red‑blue colouring of the edges of K_N contains a monochromatic K_k. The classical probabilistic lower bound, due to Erdős (1947), uses the first moment method: colour each edge independently red with probability 1/2. The expected number of monochromatic K_k is (N choose k)·21−(k choose 2). If this expectation is less than 1, there exists a colouring with no monochromatic K_k, giving R(k,k) > N. Solving yields R(k,k) > (1+o(1)) (k / e√2) 2k/2. This bound has resisted improvement for decades; the best known asymptotic improvement is a constant factor in the base of the exponent (Conlon 2009, using the alteration method).

The alteration method strengthens the first moment bound by first taking a random colouring, then deleting one vertex from each monochromatic K_k. The expected number of deletions is the expected number of monochromatic K_k, which is small when N is below the threshold. The remaining graph has no monochromatic K_k and retains most vertices, yielding a slightly larger lower bound. Conlon’s refinement uses a two‑stage alteration: first delete vertices from a sparse random subgraph, then apply the LLL to the remaining dense part. This pushes the constant factor to (1+o(1)) (k / e) 2k/2, the current record.

Explicit constructions of Ramsey graphs (colourings with no large monochromatic cliques) are much harder. The best explicit lower bounds come from algebraic constructions: the Paley graph of order q (q prime power, q ≡ 1 mod 4) gives a red‑blue colouring of K_q with no monochromatic Kc log q for some constant c. This yields R(k,k) > 2c k for some c > 0, far weaker than the probabilistic bound. Recent work on “pseudo‑random” graphs and the use of the container method has produced explicit colourings with no monochromatic Kk for N = 2Ω(k / log k), still far from the probabilistic bound. The gap between probabilistic existence and explicit construction remains a central open problem.

In hypergraph Ramsey theory, the probabilistic method gives lower bounds for R_r(k) (the smallest N such that any r‑colouring of the k‑subsets of an N‑set contains a monochromatic k‑set). The first moment method yields R_r(k) > (1+o(1)) (k / (e r1/(k−1))) rk/(k−1). The alteration method and the LLL have been used to improve the constant factors, but the exponential dependence on k remains. The best known upper bounds come from the hypergraph regularity lemma and are of tower type, leaving a vast gap.

Hypergraph Regularity and Probabilistic Embedding Techniques

The hypergraph regularity lemma, developed by Gowers (2007) and independently by Rödl, Schacht, Skokan, and others, extends Szemerédi’s graph regularity lemma to k‑uniform hypergraphs. It partitions the vertex set into a bounded number of parts such that most k‑tuples of parts are “regular” in the sense that the edge density of the hypergraph restricted to those parts is close to the global density, and this regularity is robust under further refinement. The lemma is a powerful structural tool, but its bounds are of tower height k, making it ineffective for many quantitative applications.

Probabilistic embedding techniques circumvent the tower‑type bounds by using random sampling to find a “regular” substructure of manageable size. The key idea, pioneered by Conlon, Fox, and Zhao (2014), is to first apply the regularity lemma to a dense hypergraph, then randomly sample a small subset of vertices. With high probability, the induced subhypergraph inherits a weaker form of regularity (called “weak regularity” or “ε‑regularity”) that suffices for embedding a given bounded‑degree hypergraph H. This approach yields polynomial‑type bounds for the Ramsey number of bounded‑degree hypergraphs: R(H) ≤ 2O(|V(H)|) for any k‑uniform hypergraph H with maximum degree Δ, where the constant depends only on k and Δ.

Another probabilistic embedding tool is the “random greedy embedding” algorithm. Given a host hypergraph G that is (ε, d)‑regular and a bounded‑degree hypergraph H, one embeds H into G by processing the vertices of H in a random order, at each step choosing a random image from the set of candidates that maintain the embedding constraints. The analysis uses the differential equation method to track the number of available candidates for each unembedded vertex. Concentration follows from Azuma’s inequality applied to the vertex‑exposure martingale. This yields an algorithm that finds a copy of H in G with high probability, provided G satisfies a suitable minimum codegree condition.

These techniques have been applied to prove the existence of “universal” hypergraphs (containing all bounded‑degree hypergraphs of a given size), to establish the “Kohayakawa–Łuczak–Rödl conjecture” for sparse random hypergraphs, and to give new proofs of the hypergraph removal lemma with improved bounds. The interplay between regularity (a deterministic structural decomposition) and probabilistic sampling (which extracts a well‑behaved substructure) is a recurring theme in modern extremal combinatorics.

  • Confusing the Rödl nibble with a purely greedy algorithm; the nibble uses random sampling in rounds, not a single deterministic pass.
  • Assuming the container lemma gives exact counts; it only provides an upper bound via a covering family, and the containers may overlap.
  • Overlooking the requirement that the LLL weights x_i must lie in (0,1) and satisfy the product condition; using the symmetric condition ep(d+1) ≤ 1 when the general condition is needed can give a false negative.
  • Misapplying the first moment method to Ramsey lower bounds by forgetting to check that the expectation is strictly less than 1, not just ≤ 1.
  • Treating the hypergraph regularity lemma as having polynomial bounds; its bounds are of tower height k, which is crucial for quantitative applications.
  • Neglecting the codegree conditions in the container lemma; the supersaturation step requires control of codegrees to bound the fingerprint size.
  • Believing entropy compression only works for the variable model; it extends to any algorithm with a suitable witness tree structure.

hand/waves-oscillations.html:
Coupled Oscillators and Normal Mode Analysis

When two or more oscillators interact through a coupling element — a spring, a magnetic field, or a shared medium — the system no longer oscillates at the individual natural frequencies. Instead, the equations of motion form a linear system that can be diagonalised by a suitable coordinate transformation. For two identical masses m connected by three springs of constants k (outer) and kc (central), the Lagrangian yields the coupled equations mẍ₁ = −(k+kc)x₁ + kcx₂ and mẍ₂ = kcx₁ − (k+kc)x₂. Introducing normal coordinates Q₁ = (x₁+x₂)/√2 and Q₂ = (x₁−x₂)/√2 decouples the system into two independent simple harmonic oscillators with frequencies ω₁ = √(k/m) (in‑phase mode) and ω₂ = √((k+2kc)/m) (out‑of‑phase mode). The general motion is a superposition of these normal modes, each with its own amplitude and phase determined by initial conditions.

The normal‑mode approach extends to N coupled oscillators, leading to an eigenvalue problem Ka = ω²Ma, where K is the stiffness matrix and M the mass matrix. The eigenvectors a give the spatial pattern of each mode, and the eigenvalues give the squared normal frequencies. For a uniform chain of N masses with nearest‑neighbour springs, the dispersion relation is ω(q) = 2√(k/m)|sin(qa/2)|, where q = nπ/((N+1)a) are the allowed wavevectors imposed by fixed ends. This discrete model underlies the phonon spectrum of crystals and the vibrational modes of molecules.

Energy exchange between coupled oscillators — beats — occurs when the system is prepared in a state that is not a pure normal mode. If only one oscillator is displaced initially, the energy oscillates between the two with a beat frequency Δω = ω₂−ω₁. The beat period Tbeat = 2π/Δω can be measured experimentally and used to infer the coupling strength kc. In electrical circuits, capacitive or inductive coupling between LC resonators produces identical mathematics, with the normal modes corresponding to symmetric and antisymmetric current distributions.

Applications range from mechanical vibration absorbers (tuned mass dampers) to quantum information processing, where coupled superconducting qubits are described by the same Hamiltonian. In all cases, the key steps are: write the equations of motion, construct the matrices, solve the eigenvalue problem, and interpret the eigenvectors as collective coordinates. Mastery of this procedure allows rapid analysis of any linearly coupled oscillator network.

Dispersion Relations and Group Velocity in Waveguides

A waveguide — whether a hollow metal pipe, a dielectric optical fibre, or a water channel — supports propagating modes only when the transverse boundary conditions quantise the transverse wavenumber. For a rectangular metallic waveguide of dimensions a × b (with a > b), the transverse electric (TE) and transverse magnetic (TM) modes have cutoff wavenumbers kc = √((mπ/a)² + (nπ/b)²), where m, n are non‑negative integers (not both zero for TE). The dispersion relation for a mode is ω² = c²(kz² + kc²), where kz is the longitudinal wavenumber. Below cutoff (ω < c kc), kz becomes imaginary and the field decays exponentially — the mode is evanescent.

The phase velocity vp = ω/kz = c/√(1−(ωc/ω)²) exceeds c, while the group velocity vg = dω/dkz = c√(1−(ωc/ω)²) is always less than c. Energy and information travel at the group velocity. Near cutoff, vg → 0, causing strong pulse broadening and large dispersion. The group‑velocity dispersion parameter β₂ = d²kz/dω² determines how a pulse of bandwidth Δω spreads after distance L: Δτ ≈ |β₂| L Δω. In optical fibres, material dispersion and waveguide dispersion combine; the zero‑dispersion wavelength (≈1.3 µm for standard silica) is chosen for long‑haul communication to minimise pulse spreading.

For a dielectric slab waveguide (planar optical fibre), the dispersion relation is obtained from the transcendental equation tan(κd) = 2κγ/(κ²−γ²) for symmetric TE modes, where κ = √(n₁²k₀²−β²) and γ = √(β²−n₂²k₀²), with β the propagation constant, k₀ = ω/c, and n₁, n₂ the core and cladding indices. Numerical solution yields β(ω), from which vg = (dβ/dω)⁻¹ follows. Single‑mode operation requires the normalized frequency V = k₀d√(n₁²−n₂²) < π/2. The effective index neff = β/k₀ lies between n₂ and n₁ and determines the mode confinement.

In acoustic waveguides (e.g., ducts with rigid walls), the same mathematics applies with sound speed c replacing the speed of light. Higher‑order modes have cutoff frequencies fc = (c/2)√((m/a)²+(n/b)²). Below the first cutoff, only the plane‑wave mode propagates, giving a non‑dispersive channel. This principle is used in mufflers and musical wind instruments, where the bore geometry selects the propagating modes and shapes the timbre.

Worked Example: Group Velocity in a Rectangular Waveguide
A TE₁₀ mode propagates in a rectangular waveguide with a = 2.5 cm, b = 1.2 cm at a frequency of 10 GHz. Compute the cutoff frequency, the guide wavelength, and the group velocity.
Cutoff wavenumber kc = π/a = π/0.025 = 125.66 rad/m. Cutoff frequency fc = c kc/(2π) = (3×10⁸ × 125.66)/(2π) ≈ 6.0 GHz. Since f = 10 GHz > fc, the mode propagates. Free‑space wavenumber k₀ = 2πf/c = 2π×10¹⁰/3×10⁸ ≈ 209.44 rad/m. Longitudinal wavenumber kz = √(k₀²−kc²) = √(209.44²−125.66²) ≈ 167.55 rad/m. Guide wavelength λg = 2π/kz ≈ 0.0375 m = 3.75 cm. Group velocity vg = c² kz/ω = c √(1−(fc/f)²) = 3×10⁸ √(1−0.6²) = 3×10⁸ × 0.8 = 2.4×10⁸ m/s.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a waveguide problem asks for group velocity, first compute the cutoff frequency from the geometry and mode indices. Then use vg = c √(1−(fc/f)²) for rectangular guides; for dielectric guides, differentiate the numerical β(ω) curve or use the approximate formula vg ≈ c/(neff + ω dneff/dω). Remember that phase velocity exceeds c but carries no information — only group velocity matters for pulse propagation.

Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation and Optical Solitons

The nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE) i∂ψ/∂z + (1/2)∂²ψ/∂t² + |ψ|²ψ = 0 governs the slow envelope ψ(z,t) of a quasi‑monochromatic pulse in a Kerr medium, where the refractive index n = n₀ + n₂I depends on intensity I. The first term describes diffraction (or dispersion in the temporal domain), the second term is group‑velocity dispersion (GVD), and the third term is the cubic nonlinearity. In anomalous dispersion regime (β₂ < 0), the dispersive broadening ∝ β₂ is exactly balanced by self‑phase modulation ∝ n₂, yielding a stable solitary wave — a fundamental soliton.

The fundamental soliton solution is ψ(z,t) = η sech(η t) exp(i η² z/2), where η is the inverse pulse width and also the peak amplitude (in normalized units). Its energy (or pulse power) is fixed: P = 2η. Higher‑order solitons (N‑solitons) have integer N > 1 and exhibit periodic breathing with period z₀ = π/2η². The inverse scattering transform (IST) provides the exact multi‑soliton solutions and shows that solitons emerge from arbitrary initial pulses through a process called soliton fission, accompanied by dispersive radiation.

In optical fibres, the physical NLSE includes higher‑order effects: third‑order dispersion (β₃), self‑steepening (∂/∂t(|ψ|²ψ)), and Raman scattering (delayed nonlinear response). These perturbations cause soliton self‑frequency shift (toward longer wavelengths) and can lead to soliton fission in supercontinuum generation. The soliton order N = √(γ P₀ T₀²/|β₂|) determines the dynamics; for N ≫ 1, the pulse breaks into N fundamental solitons. Practical fibre communication uses fundamental solitons (N = 1) at 1.55 µm where silica has anomalous dispersion and low loss.

Beyond fibres, the NLSE describes Bose‑Einstein condensates (Gross‑Pitaevskii equation), water waves in shallow tanks, and plasma waves. The common mathematical structure — integrability via IST — guarantees elastic collisions: solitons pass through each other preserving shape and velocity, acquiring only a phase shift. This particle‑like behaviour underpins proposals for all‑optical logic gates and soliton‑based quantum computing.

Acoustic Impedance Matching and Reflection Coefficients

When a sound wave encounters an interface between two media with characteristic acoustic impedances Z₁ = ρ₁c₁ and Z₂ = ρ₂c₂, part of the wave is reflected and part transmitted. For normal incidence, the pressure reflection coefficient is R = (Z₂−Z₁)/(Z₂+Z₁) and the transmission coefficient is T = 2Z₂/(Z₂+Z₁). The intensity reflection coefficient is |R|², and the intensity transmission coefficient is (Z₁/Z₂)|T|² = 4Z₁Z₂/(Z₁+Z₂)². If Z₁ = Z₂, R = 0 and all energy is transmitted — perfect impedance matching.

For oblique incidence at angle θ₁, Snell’s law gives sinθ₁/c₁ = sinθ₂/c₂. The reflection coefficient for pressure becomes R(θ₁) = (Z₂ cosθ₁ − Z₁ cosθ₂)/(Z₂ cosθ₁ + Z₁ cosθ₂). At the critical angle θc = arcsin(c₁/c₂) (when c₂ > c₁), the transmitted wave becomes evanescent and |R| = 1 — total internal reflection. This principle is used in ultrasonic non‑destructive testing to detect flaws by analysing reflected echoes.

Quarter‑wave matching layers provide broadband impedance matching. A layer of thickness λ/4 and impedance Zm = √(Z₁Z₂) inserted between the two media yields zero reflection at the design frequency. Multi‑layer stacks (e.g., binomial or Chebyshev transformers) broaden the bandwidth. In medical ultrasound transducers, a matching layer between the piezoelectric ceramic (Z ≈ 30 MRayl) and tissue (Z ≈ 1.5 MRayl) dramatically improves transmission efficiency and signal‑to‑noise ratio.

Transmission line theory provides an exact electrical analogue: voltage pressure, current volume velocity, characteristic impedance Z₀ = √(L/C). The same reflection coefficient formula applies, and Smith chart techniques can be used to design matching networks. This cross‑disciplinary equivalence allows microwave engineers to solve acoustic matching problems and vice‑versa.

Parametric Resonance and the Mathieu Equation

Parametric resonance occurs when a system parameter — such as the length of a pendulum, the stiffness of a spring, or the capacitance in an LC circuit — is modulated periodically at twice the natural frequency. The canonical model is the Mathieu equation d²x/dt² + [δ + ε cos(2t)]x = 0, where δ = (ω₀/ωm)² and ε measures the modulation depth. Stability charts in the (δ, ε) plane show alternating stable and unstable tongues emanating from δ = n² (n = 1,2,…). The principal instability tongue (n = 1) is centred at δ = 1, i.e., modulation frequency ωm ≈ 2ω₀.

For a pendulum with vertically oscillating support, the effective gravity becomes geff = g + aωm² cos(ωmt), leading to the Mathieu equation with δ = 4g/(lωm²) and ε = 4a/l. When the support oscillates at twice the pendulum’s natural frequency, the upright position can become stable — the Kapitza pendulum. This counter‑intuitive stabilization is a hallmark of parametric control and finds applications in particle traps (Paul trap) and vibrational stabilization of inverted pendulums in robotics.

In electrical circuits, a varactor diode modulates the capacitance of an LC tank at 2f₀, producing parametric amplification. The Manley‑Rowe relations dictate that the signal and idler frequencies satisfy ωs + ωi = ωp (pump frequency). A degenerate parametric amplifier (ωs = ωi = ωp/2) provides phase‑sensitive gain with no added noise, reaching the quantum limit. This principle underlies Josephson parametric amplifiers used in superconducting quantum circuits for qubit readout.

Floquet theory provides the general solution for any periodic coefficient: x(t) = eμtp(t), where p(t) has the modulation period and μ is the Floquet exponent. Instability corresponds to Re(μ) > 0. Numerical computation of the monodromy matrix over one period yields the stability boundaries for arbitrary modulation waveforms, not just sinusoidal. This extends the analysis to square‑wave or pulsed parametric drives used in MEMS resonators for frequency multiplication and sensing.

  • Confusing phase velocity with group velocity in waveguide problems — remember energy travels at group velocity.
  • Assuming all coupled oscillators have the same normal‑mode frequencies — they split into symmetric and antisymmetric branches.
  • Neglecting the intensity‑dependent refractive index when estimating soliton power — the NLSE balance requires exact peak power.
  • Using the normal‑incidence reflection coefficient for oblique incidence — the angle‑dependent formula must be applied.
  • Treating parametric resonance as ordinary forced resonance — the instability condition is modulation at twice the natural frequency, not at the natural frequency.
  • Overlooking the role of the Floquet exponent in determining stability boundaries for non‑sinusoidal parametric drives.
  • Forgetting that the quarter‑wave matching layer only gives perfect matching at a single design frequency unless a multi‑layer transformer is used.

english/active-passive.html:
Causative and Quasi‑Passive Constructions

The causative verbs have, get, make, let and help generate structures that look passive but follow distinct syntactic rules. In have/get something done the object receives the action performed by an unnamed agent: She had the roof repaired. The past participle repaired functions as a complement of the object, not as a main verb, so the auxiliary be never appears. By contrast, make and let take a bare infinitive: They made him apologise; She let the children play. When these causatives are turned into the passive, the infinitive becomes a to-infinitive: He was made to apologise; The children were let to play (the latter is rare and often replaced by were allowed to play). Help permits both bare and to-infinitives in the active (He helped me move / helped me to move) but only the to-form in the passive (I was helped to move).

A frequent examination trap is the confusion between have something done (causative) and have something doing (experiential). I had my car stolen implies an external agent; I had my car stealing is ungrammatical. Another nuance: get can be used informally for the passive (He got arrested) but retains the causative sense only with a past participle complement (She got the report finished). In formal writing, have is preferred for the causative, while get signals a more colloquial register.

When a causative clause is embedded under a reporting verb, the back‑shift rules apply to the matrix verb, not to the causative complement. For example, He said he had had the fence painted (past perfect of have + past participle). The participle painted remains unchanged because it is non‑finite. Mastery of these patterns prevents the common error of inserting an auxiliary be where none belongs.

Passive of Complex and Embedded Structures

Beyond simple transitive clauses, the passive can operate on infinitival, gerundial, and participial complements. An infinitival passive appears after verbs of expectation, perception, or obligation: The report is expected to be submitted by Friday. The subject of the main clause (report) becomes the subject of the passive infinitive to be submitted. Gerundial passives occur after prepositions or verbs that license -ing forms: She dislikes being interrupted; There is no chance of the bill being passed. Here the gerund being interrupted carries the passive voice internally.

Participial clauses, both present and perfect, also admit passive morphology. A present participle passive (Being written in haste, the letter contained errors) functions as an adverbial modifier, while a perfect participle passive (Having been informed of the change, we adjusted the schedule) indicates anteriority. In reduced relative clauses, the passive participle replaces a full relative clause: The documents required for the interview (= The documents that are required). This reduction is permissible only when the relativised noun is the patient of the verb.

Embedded questions and noun clauses can be passivised when the matrix verb permits a passive complement. It is not known whether the proposal will be accepted shows a passive matrix (is not known) governing a finite clause. When the embedded clause itself is passive, the sequence of passives must respect the hierarchy of finiteness: the higher clause takes the finite passive, the lower clause remains non‑finite if it is an infinitive or gerund. Errors arise when candidates attempt to double‑passivise a finite clause, producing ungrammatical strings such as *It is believed that the treaty was been signed.

Another advanced pattern is the get-passive in complex predicates: He got his application rejected (causative) versus He got rejected (adversative passive). The latter implies an unexpected or undesirable outcome and is restricted to informal registers. In formal examinations, the be-passive remains the standard for all embedded structures.

Transformation Drill
Convert the following active sentence into a passive construction that retains the original meaning and register: The committee expects the draft to be reviewed by the legal team before submission.
Step 1: Identify the matrix verb expects (active, present simple). Step 2: The object of expects is the infinitival clause the draft to be reviewed by the legal team before submission. Step 3: Passivise the matrix clause: The draft is expected to be reviewed by the legal team before submission. The infinitival complement already contains a passive (to be reviewed), so it remains unchanged. The final passive sentence is: The draft is expected to be reviewed by the legal team before submission.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a sentence contains more than one verb, locate the finite verb first; only that verb undergoes tense back‑shift or voice change. Non‑finite complements (infinitives, gerunds, participles) keep their internal voice. Mark the finite verb, apply the passive rule to it, and leave the rest untouched.

Advanced Narration: Reporting of Modals, Conditionals, and Subjunctive Mood

Reporting verbs in the past tense trigger systematic back‑shift of modal auxiliaries. Can becomes could; may becomes might; will becomes would; shall becomes should (first person) or would (other persons); must usually becomes had to for obligation, but remains must when expressing logical deduction. Need not and dare not shift to need not have / dare not have only in perfect contexts; otherwise they stay unchanged.

Conditional sentences follow the same back‑shift hierarchy. A first conditional (If it rains, I will stay home) reported in the past becomes He said that if it rained he would stay home. The protasis shifts from present to past; the apodosis shifts from will to would. A second conditional (If I were you, I would accept) reported becomes She said that if she were me she would accept — the subjunctive were remains were because it is already past‑subjunctive. A third conditional (If he had studied, he would have passed) reported becomes They said that if he had studied he would have passed — no further shift is possible because both verbs are already past perfect / would have + past participle.

The subjunctive mood in mandative constructions (It is essential that he be present) is preserved in indirect speech when the reporting verb is in the present: She says that it is essential that he be present. With a past reporting verb, the subjunctive may be back‑shifted to a past subjunctive form (She said that it was essential that he be present) or, more commonly in modern usage, replaced by should be (She said that it was essential that he should be present). Examiners often test the distinction between be (present subjunctive) and were (past subjunctive) in reported mandatives.

Reporting of let imperatives follows a special pattern: Let us go → He suggested that they should go or He proposed going. The bare infinitive after let cannot be directly back‑shifted; a modal or gerund replaces it. Similarly, had better remains unchanged in indirect speech (He said I had better leave) because it is a semi‑modal with no past form.

Free Indirect Speech and Narrative Distance

Free indirect speech (FIS) blends the character’s voice with the narrator’s, omitting reporting clauses and quotation marks while retaining the character’s deictic centre. Example: He would not go. The rain was relentless. The first sentence reflects the character’s modal would (past of will) without a reporting verb; the second uses past tense narration but the perspective remains the character’s. FIS is identified by three markers: (1) third‑person pronouns, (2) past tense narration, (3) retention of the character’s modal, temporal, and evaluative expressions.

In examination passages, FIS often appears in comprehension questions asking for the “tone” or “point of view”. Recognising FIS prevents mis‑attributing a character’s thought to the narrator. A typical trap: the passage reads She felt that the decision was unfair — this is direct narration, not FIS, because the reporting verb felt is explicit. True FIS would read The decision was unfair. She would have to accept it.

Conversion between direct speech, indirect speech, and FIS is a higher‑order skill. Direct: “I will finish the report,” he said. Indirect: He said that he would finish the report. FIS: He would finish the report. The deadline loomed. Note the shift of the reporting clause into narrative description and the preservation of the modal would. Examiners may ask to rewrite a paragraph in FIS to test control of deictic shifting.

Voice and Narration in Formal and Legal Discourse

Legal drafting favours the passive to emphasise the action over the agent: The contract shall be executed by the parties. The modal shall expresses obligation; its passive form shall be executed is standard. In statutory interpretation, the passive can create ambiguity about the duty‑bearer, prompting courts to apply the “presumption of agency” — the entity with the power to act is presumed to be the agent.

Judicial orders frequently use the let construction for directives: Let the respondent file a reply within thirty days. When reported, this becomes The court directed that the respondent should file a reply within thirty days. The subjunctive should replaces the imperative let. Similarly, legislative texts employ it is hereby enacted that followed by a passive clause: It is hereby enacted that the tax shall be levied. In indirect narration of such texts, the reporting verb states or provides takes a that-clause with the original modal preserved if the reporting verb is present: The Act provides that the tax shall be levied.

International treaties illustrate the interplay of voice and narration across languages. The authentic English text may read The Parties shall cooperate; a French version uses the future indicative les Parties coopéreront. When a tribunal reports the treaty provision, it must decide whether to back‑shift the modal. The prevailing practice is to retain shall because the treaty remains in force, illustrating that back‑shift is not automatic when the reported content expresses a continuing obligation.

In administrative notices, the get-passive appears in informal guidance (You’ll get fined if you park here) but is avoided in formal orders. Recognising register‑appropriate voice choices is essential for editing tasks that ask to “improve the tone” of a passage.

  • Treating have/get something done as a regular passive and inserting be (e.g., *The roof was had repaired).
  • Failing to change the bare infinitive after make/let to a to-infinitive in the passive (e.g., *He was made apologise).
  • Double‑passivising an embedded finite clause (e.g., *It is believed that the treaty was been signed).
  • Back‑shifting a subjunctive be to was in mandative reports (e.g., *She said it was essential that he was present).
  • Converting a third conditional into a second conditional during narration (e.g., *He said if he studied he would pass instead of if he had studied he would have passed).
  • Misidentifying free indirect speech as direct narration because of retained modals, leading to wrong attribution in comprehension questions.
  • Using the get-passive in formal legal editing tasks where the be-passive is required.
The advanced patterns above complete the toolkit needed for high‑level voice and narration questions.

hand/siegel-modular-forms.html:
Fourier–Jacobi Expansions and the Maass Space

The Fourier–Jacobi expansion of a Siegel modular form of degree two writes the form as a series in the variable τ (the upper‑left entry of the period matrix) whose coefficients are Jacobi forms of increasing index. Concretely, for Z = (τ, z; z, ω) in the Siegel upper half‑space ℌ₂, a Siegel modular form F of weight k admits an expansion F(Z) = Σm≥0 φ_m(τ, z) e2π i m ω, where each φ_m is a Jacobi form of weight k and index m. This decomposition is the higher‑genus analogue of the classical Fourier expansion of elliptic modular forms and is indispensable for studying the structure of the Maass space M_k^*(Γ₂). The Maass space consists precisely of those Siegel cusp forms whose Fourier coefficients A(T) depend only on the discriminant D = b²−4ac and the content gcd(a,b,c) of the binary quadratic form T = ((a, b/2), (b/2, c)). Equivalently, a form lies in the Maass space iff its Fourier–Jacobi coefficients φ_m are all lifts of a single elliptic cusp form via the classical Maass lift. The Maass lift sends a Hecke eigenform f ∈ S2k−2(SL₂(ℤ)) to a Siegel cusp form F ∈ S_k(Γ₂) whose Fourier–Jacobi coefficients are the Jacobi forms obtained from f by the Eichler–Zagier construction. This lift coincides with the Saito–Kurokawa lift, and the equality of the two descriptions is a theorem of Maass, Andrianov, and Zagier. The Fourier–Jacobi expansion also makes visible the action of the Hecke operators on the Maass space: the Hecke algebra on S_k(Γ₂) preserves the subspace, and its eigenvalues on the Maass space are exactly the eigenvalues of the corresponding elliptic Hecke operators on f, together with the trivial eigenvalues coming from the symmetric square L‑function. This compatibility underlies the proof that the spinor L‑function of a Saito–Kurokawa lift factors as L(f, s) ζ(s−k+1) ζ(s−k+2). Moreover, the Fourier–Jacobi expansion provides a practical tool for computing Fourier coefficients of lifted forms, because the coefficients of the Jacobi forms φ_m are given by explicit formulas involving the Fourier coefficients of f and divisor sums. In particular, for a fundamental discriminant D < 0, the coefficient A(T) with discriminant D equals Σd|gcd(a,b,c) dk−1 a(|D|/d²). This formula is the starting point for many numerical verifications of the paramodular conjecture and for the construction of explicit examples of Siegel modular forms that are not lifts.

Theta Lifts and the Weil Representation

The theta correspondence, also known as the Howe duality, furnishes a powerful method to lift automorphic forms from a smaller group to a larger one by integrating against a theta kernel. In the Siegel setting, the dual pair (Sp(2g), O(V)) inside the symplectic group Sp(2g·dim V) gives rise to a Weil representation ω_ψ of the metaplectic double cover Mp(2g·dim V). For a quadratic space V over ℚ of dimension m, the theta kernel Θ_φ(g, h) = Σx∈V(ℚ) ω_ψ(g, h) φ(x) (with φ a Schwartz–Bruhat function) is an automorphic form on the product of the adelic points of Sp(2g) and O(V). Integrating Θ_φ against a cusp form on O(V) yields a Siegel modular form on Sp(2g); conversely, integrating against a Siegel modular form produces an automorphic form on O(V). This construction is functorial with respect to the Langlands parameters: the standard L‑function of the lifted Siegel form is the product of the standard L‑function of the original form and a product of Riemann zeta factors determined by the representation of the dual group. The most classical instance is the Shimura correspondence, which lifts half‑integral weight modular forms (automorphic forms on the metaplectic cover of SL₂) to integral weight forms on SL₂ via the theta kernel attached to the quadratic form Q(x) = x². For higher genus, the theta lift from O(2) to Sp(4) recovers the Saito–Kurokawa lift, while the lift from O(3) to Sp(4) produces the Yoshida lift, which attaches a Siegel modular form of degree two to a pair of elliptic cusp forms of weights k₁ and k₂. The Weil representation also underlies the Siegel–Weil formula, which expresses the Siegel Eisenstein series as an integral of the theta kernel over the orthogonal group. This identity provides the analytic continuation and functional equation of the Eisenstein series and relates its Fourier coefficients to representation numbers of quadratic forms. In the arithmetic setting, the Kudla program interprets the Fourier coefficients of the derivative of the Eisenstein series at its central point as intersection numbers of special cycles on Shimura varieties, thereby linking the theta lift to arithmetic geometry. The theta correspondence is thus a unifying mechanism that connects Siegel modular forms with orthogonal modular forms, half‑integral weight forms, and the geometry of Shimura varieties.

Worked Example: Computing a Fourier–Jacobi Coefficient
Let f(τ) = Σn≥1 a(n) qⁿ be the normalized Hecke eigenform of weight 12 for SL₂(ℤ) (the Ramanujan Δ‑function). Using the Maass lift, construct the Siegel cusp form F ∈ S₁₀(Γ₂). Compute the Fourier coefficient A(T) for T = ((2, 1), (1, 3)).
The matrix T has a = 2, b = 2, c = 3. Its discriminant is D = b² − 4ac = 4 − 24 = −20. The content g = gcd(a, b, c) = gcd(2, 2, 3) = 1. The Maass lift formula gives A(T) = Σd|g dk−1 a(|D|/d²) with k = 10. Since g = 1, the only divisor is d = 1. Thus A(T) = 1⁹ · a(20). The Fourier coefficient a(20) of Δ is known to be −288. Therefore A(T) = −288.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for a Fourier coefficient of a Saito–Kurokawa lift, first compute the discriminant and content of the given binary quadratic form. Then apply the divisor sum formula using the weight of the Siegel form (k) and the known coefficients of the underlying elliptic eigenform. Memorise the first few coefficients of Δ (weight 12) and of the weight 16 and 18 eigenforms, as they appear frequently in numerical problems.

The Paramodular Conjecture and Abelian Surfaces

The paramodular conjecture, formulated by Brumer and Kramer, predicts a precise correspondence between isogeny classes of abelian surfaces over ℚ with endomorphism ring ℤ and Siegel paramodular newforms of degree two with rational Hecke eigenvalues. A paramodular form is a Siegel modular form for the paramodular group K(N) ⊂ Sp(4, ℚ), which is the stabiliser of a certain lattice chain; its level N is the conductor of the abelian surface. The conjecture asserts that for each such abelian surface A/ℚ there exists a unique paramodular newform F of weight 2 and level N such that the L‑function of A coincides with the spinor L‑function of F, and conversely every paramodular newform with rational eigenvalues arises in this way. This is the genus‑two analogue of the modularity theorem for elliptic curves (the Taniyama–Shimura–Weil conjecture). Substantial evidence includes the verification for all paramodular forms of level up to 1000 by Poor and Yuen, and the proof of the conjecture for abelian surfaces with real multiplication by a quadratic field (the Hilbert modular case) by Zhang and others. The paramodular group K(N) is defined as the set of matrices in Sp(4, ℚ) that preserve the lattice ℤ ⊕ ℤ ⊕ Nℤ ⊕ Nℤ and its dual; its Fourier expansion involves a character that distinguishes it from the full Siegel modular group. The Hecke operators at primes p ∤ N act on the space of paramodular forms and their eigenvalues are expected to match the Frobenius traces on the ℓ‑adic Tate module of the abelian surface. The conjecture also predicts that the spinor L‑function of a paramodular newform has an Euler product of degree four with the expected functional equation and that the central critical value L(F, 1) is related to the order of the Tate–Shafarevich group of the abelian surface via the Bloch–Kato conjecture. Recent work by Boxer, Calegari, Gee, and Pilloni has established potential modularity for many abelian surfaces, bringing the full conjecture within reach of the Taylor–Wiles method. The paramodular conjecture thus sits at the intersection of the Langlands program for GSp(4), the arithmetic of abelian varieties, and the theory of Siegel modular forms for non‑maximal level subgroups.

Ikeda Lifts and Higher Degree Generalizations

The Ikeda lift, introduced by Tamotsu Ikeda in 2001, generalises the Saito–Kurokawa lift from degree two to arbitrary genus n. Given a normalized Hecke eigenform f ∈ S2k(SL₂(ℤ)) of even weight 2k, the Ikeda lift produces a Siegel cusp form I_n(f) ∈ Sk+n−1(Sp(2n, ℤ)). The weight shift k+n−1 reflects the fact that the lift lands in the holomorphic discrete series representation of Sp(2n, ℝ) with minimal K‑type. The standard L‑function of the lifted form factorises as L(I_n(f), s, St) = L(f, s) ∏j=1n−1 ζ(2s−2j). This factorisation shows that the lift corresponds to the functorial transfer from GL₂ to GSp(2n) associated to the symmetric square representation of the L‑group. The Fourier coefficients of I_n(f) are given by an explicit formula involving the Fourier coefficients a(m) of f and the representation numbers of quadratic forms of rank n. For a positive definite half‑integral matrix T of size n, the coefficient A(T) equals Σd|e(T) dk+n−2 a(det(2T)/d²) where e(T) is the content of T. When n = 2 this reduces to the Saito–Kurokawa formula. The Ikeda lift is injective and its image is characterised as the subspace of Siegel cusp forms whose Fourier coefficients depend only on the GL_n(ℤ)‑equivalence class of T; this generalises the Maass space characterisation. The lift also respects Hecke eigenvalues: for p prime, the Satake parameters of I_n(f) are {α_p, β_p, pk−1, pk−2, …, pk−n} where α_p, β_p are the Satake parameters of f. This compatibility with the local Langlands correspondence for GSp(2n) is a key piece of evidence for the global Langlands functoriality conjecture. Beyond the Ikeda lift, there are further generalisations such as the Böcherer–Schulze‑Pillot lift from orthogonal modular forms to Siegel modular forms, and the endoscopic lifts constructed by Arthur using the trace formula. These lifts populate the discrete spectrum of Sp(2n) and provide explicit examples of CAP (cuspidal associated to parabolic) representations, which are central to the classification of automorphic representations of symplectic groups.

Arithmetic of Siegel Modular Forms: L‑functions and Special Values

The arithmetic significance of Siegel modular forms is largely encoded in their L‑functions. For a Siegel cusp form F of degree g, there are several natural L‑functions: the spinor L‑function Z_F(s) (degree 2^g), the standard L‑function L(F, s, St) (degree 2g+1), and the adjoint L‑function L(F, s, Ad) (degree (2g+1)(g+1)/2). For g = 2, the spinor L‑function has an Euler product Z_F(s) = ∏_p Q_p(p−s)−1 where Q_p(X) = (1−α_p X)(1−α_p-1β_p X)(1−β_p-1γ_p X)(1−γ_p X) and the Satake parameters α_p, β_p, γ_p satisfy α_p β_p γ_p = p2k−3. The standard L‑function is L(F, s, St) = ∏_p (1−α_p p−s)−1(1−β_p p−s)−1(1−γ_p p−s)−1(1−p−s)−1(1−p1−s)−1. When F is a Saito–Kurokawa lift of an elliptic eigenform f, the spinor L‑function factors as L(f, s) ζ(s−k+1) ζ(s−k+2) and the standard L‑function factors as L(f, s) ζ(s−k+1) ζ(s−k+2) ζ(s−2k+3). The critical values of these L‑functions are expected to be algebraic multiples of periods, and the Bloch–Kato conjecture predicts that the leading term at the central point s = k is related to the order of a Selmer group attached to the motive of F. For paramodular forms corresponding to abelian surfaces, the spinor L‑function coincides with the Hasse–Weil L‑function of the surface, and the Birch and Swinnerton‑Dyer conjecture translates into a formula for L(F, 1) in terms of the regulator, Tamagawa numbers, and the Tate–Shafarevich group. The Gan–Gross–Prasad conjecture for the pair (GSpin(5), GSpin(4)) predicts the non‑vanishing of certain period integrals of Siegel modular forms, which in turn implies the non‑vanishing of central L‑values for twists by quadratic characters. This has been used to prove cases of the Birch and Swinnerton‑Dyer conjecture for abelian surfaces with real multiplication. The Kudla program provides a geometric interpretation of the Fourier coefficients of the derivative of the Siegel Eisenstein series at s = 0 as heights of special cycles on Shimura varieties, leading to a conjectural formula for the central derivative of the spinor L‑function. These deep connections place Siegel modular forms at the heart of modern arithmetic geometry and the Langlands program.

  • Confusing the Maass space with the full space of Siegel cusp forms; the Maass space is a proper subspace characterised by Fourier coefficients depending only on the GL₂(ℤ)‑orbit of T.
  • Assuming the Saito–Kurokawa lift is surjective onto all Siegel cusp forms of weight k; it is injective but its image is exactly the Maass space, which has codimension growing with k.
  • Misapplying the Fourier–Jacobi expansion by treating the Jacobi index m as the discriminant of T; the index equals the lower‑right entry of T, not the discriminant.
  • Overlooking the level structure in the paramodular conjecture; paramodular forms live on K(N), not on the full Siegel modular group, and their Hecke eigenvalues at primes dividing N differ from the unramified case.
  • Confusing the Ikeda lift weight formula; the target weight is k+n−1, not k+n or 2k−2.
  • Neglecting the distinction between spinor and standard L‑functions; they have different degrees and different factorisations under lifts.
  • Treating the theta lift as always producing a cusp form; the theta lift of a non‑cuspidal form can be an Eisenstein series, and the Siegel–Weil formula precisely relates the two.
